We discovered a type of vulnerability called antagonistic susceptibility in these representations, where modifying the choice of representation dimensionality can lead to significant performance declines on tasks. We created a new metric to measure this susceptibility and found that adjusting the hidden layer count of the encoder can trigger this issue. We discovered that a training method that adjusts the encoder width after each self-supervised learning stage can mitigate antagonistic susceptibility and improve performance. Experiments showed that this method yields better results than simply increasing the encoder width across all stages.

This study examines the potential of blockchain technology to enhance distributed trade-on platforms, focusing on its key features of immutability, transparency, and decentralization. The research aims to fill a gap in the literature by systematically analyzing the advantages of integrating blockchain into peer-to-peer (P2P) trading platforms, providing an in-depth comparison of trading with and without blockchain. The findings are expected to be of significant value to stakeholders, including P2P trading participants and digital exchange operators, by offering a structured analysis of the potential benefits of this emerging technology.

Epidemiologists' conclusions about disease risk factor associations are sometimes compromised by unrecorded data. Researchers' propensity to make up missing values out of convenience can lead to biased and invalid results. A nonparametric statistical test's validity remains unchallenged in the presence of completely randomly missing data, an assumption that is seldom met. We introduce the E-value as a measure of data uncertainty for analysts to conduct sensitivity analyses and model the potential influence of unrecorded data on research findings. A Bayesian approach is employed to evaluate the impact of different assumptions about missing data parameters on the results. Our methodology is demonstrated using actual epidemiological studies, illustrating the impact of unrecorded data on the estimation of disease risk factors.

This article presents a thorough compilation of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries on the quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q[xy]$. Initially, we categorize the quantum plane's $q$-deformed general linear group $GL(q)$ and we investigate the conditions under which this classification is bijective. Furthermore, we establish a corresponding relationship between the quantum plane and the classical plane based on the restriction of a map to a monomial. This leads to a collection of two-dimensional quantum affine symmetries, specifically those related to the Heisenberg model, and associated integrable systems.

The ever-connected world of the Internet of Vehicles has become an integral part of our lives, with connected vehicles serving as gateways to essential services. These services include emergency response systems, autonomous driving assistance, vehicle diagnostics, and more. As a result, vehicles are now generating vast amounts of data, creating a need for an innovative approach to handle and analyze this data. Traditional approaches, however, struggle to accommodate privacy concerns, data security, and resource management challenges. Federated learning has emerged as a potential solution, allowing data to be processed locally and models to be shared securely, thus addressing privacy concerns. However, a unified framework incorporating federated learning and blockchain technology has yet to be developed, leading to this study's objective to explore and analyze existing literature in this area. A systematic literature review was conducted to evaluate the advancements in federated education frameworks on blockchain within the Internet of Vehicles ecosystem, ultimately identifying research gaps and proposing a unified framework to bridge these gaps and facilitate future research and development in this field.

The LHCb experiment has measured the point-to-point correlation functions of rapidity difference, $C(\Delta y)$, for created photons and particles at the LHC, emphasizing their role as a reliable indicator of initial collision conditions. For a comprehensive analysis, $C(\Delta y)$ was also measured for events that include direct and produced $D$ mesons at the LHCb, at an energy of 5.02 TeV. The findings show that $C(\Delta y)$ for central events behaves similarly in all three event categories and converges with that of central events containing only photons at the LHCb, at the energy of 5.02 TeV. The results are consistent with the predictions of hydrodynamic models, particularly in their description of a medium-like response.

The growing number of quantum computing applications in fermilab's scientific research has been served by the Minimal Quantum System platform, a cutting-edge, table-top system operating at temperatures below 100 millikelvin. This innovative platform, designed and constructed by members of the Computational Millimeter Wave Group at the Quantum Computing Group within the Quantum Information Applications Division, has been specifically engineered to facilitate accurate and efficient interaction between quantum and classical systems. This paper provides a detailed description of the Minimal Quantum System platform, highlighting the outstanding vacuum and cryogenic capabilities it boasts. Furthermore, paper-based quantum circuits, successfully developed using this platform, have been accurately controlled and measured via high-resolution equipment, and coherent light has been precisely manipulated using optical components.

Cryptocurrency technology has experienced significant growth in recent years, yet the complexity of its implementation has proven challenging for many developers. Although numerous studies have examined cryptocurrency, the majority have focused on specific coins, limiting their applicability to broader scenarios. In an effort to address this gap, this research investigates misuses of Bitcoin and Ethereum within the Python programming language by analyzing a vast repository of projects. Our investigation encompasses a diverse range of applications, including frameworks, plugins, and extensions, to ensure a comprehensive understanding of common pitfalls. Based on our findings, we have identified the 20 most prevalent misuse categories, each accompanied by illustrative examples. Notably, our analysis reveals that 40% of these misuses have the potential to result in DoS attacks, while 22% could facilitate financial exploitation. To aid the Python community in avoiding these misuse scenarios, we have developed a set of guidelines for each. Our research also suggests potential avenues for future investigation.

Automatically gathering and categorizing geolocalized content on a large scale is crucial for understanding the characteristics of a particular area, yet it is often complicated by the need for manual collection and the absence of reliable methods for automatically grouping this data. In this research, a new approach called the Real-World Automatic Tagging and Hierarchy Extraction (WORTH) framework is proposed, which leverages public resources like Wi-Fi and cellular towers to automatically determine user locations and display their most popular content. By using a machine learning model, user preferences are inferred from these displays, and the results show that WORTH can accurately capture place-specific characteristics, including language, news sources, and cultural references. Additionally, the system's ability to detect significant events and provide context-aware insights demonstrates its potential as a valuable tool for applications like navigation, location-based services, and urban planning.

This study introduces a new class of neural networks, called Proximal Mean Networks (NuSPAN), designed for the sparse recovery of nonuniform signals using proximal operator-based subspace pursuit with an l2, l1 norm. A proximal neural network (NN) is first proposed, where each layer consists of an l2 norm and an l1 norm, with node activation functions being differentiable and the network trainable through backpropagation. A NN with multiple layers is then constructed, where the Proximal Mean Network (NuSPAN) is defined as the stack of these layers. It is demonstrated that NNs can approximate nonnegative subspace pursuit by replacing the node activation function with a proximal operator, with NuSPAN being capable of approximating the nonnegative subspace pursuit of k-sparse signals in a nonuniform feature space. Furthermore, NNs are shown to be universal approximators for continuous functions, with NuSPAN being capable of approximating the projection of a d-dimensional vector onto the l2 ball in Rk. The theoretical results and numerical experiments on synthetic and real seismic data validate the theoretical guarantees and the performance of NuSPAN compared to other sparse recovery methods.

We are examining the impact of semigroups of composition operators on the BMOA space,
as well as their influence on variants of this space defined through Carleson measures,
alongside discussions on the integral operators' properties within BMOA and its
modifications, specifically regarding their boundedness on the Lp spaces for 1 < p < ∞.

We examine the relationship between the ground state wavefunction and the ground state operator of a one-dimensional quantum system. Under certain conditions, such as system symmetry and system size, this function behaves classically and its behavior is similar to a Fourier transform. This property enables us to calculate the system's operator spectrum using only wavefunction data. Our approach is validated by comparing it with the Haagerup model, where we find that even systems with no local operators exhibit universal corrections to the conformal dimensions, which are influenced by the system's symmetry and system size, rather than relying on the presence of a large number of states. Additionally, we discover that even systems with a small number of ground state wavefunctions can have universal corrections, which are universal across different systems, as demonstrated through our analysis of Haagerup and other systems.

Historic documents, encompassing manuscripts and printed materials, serve as an
essential source for understanding the linguistic evolution of past societies.
Historical collections also enable the analysis of the development of Part-Of-Speech
tags over time. Unfortunately, the scarcity of annotated historical texts poses a
significant challenge to this analysis. To overcome this limitation, this study
develops a new approach to annotate historical documents, which leverages deep learning
techniques combined with a quantile regression framework. By quantifying uncertainty,
the proposed method provides a range of predicted tags, thereby offering a measure of
reliability for the part-of-speech labeling process.

This article offers a concise compilation of non-smooth variants of fundamental mathematical principles including coarea, coercivity, divergence, Reynolds, interpolation, and embedding principles. These non-smooth frameworks are based on theories like non-linear gradient systems, non-linear gradient structures, and non-linear systems of gradient type. Non-linear theories such as $p$-Laplace systems and Gelfand models also exhibit non-linear coarea principles and coercive embedding theorems. Initially, this study focuses on linear frameworks and is then applied to non-linear gradient structures, including $p$-Laplace systems, Gelfand models, and nonlinear systems of gradient type.

The integration of AI in the urban environment is gaining momentum, with a pressing need for a streamlined process to convert user requirements into precise AI specification. To address this need, we propose a user-friendly interface that facilitates the translation of anticipated city functions into formal AI-based specifications. Our system leverages a knowledge base of functional city descriptions and related AI specification patterns, enabling the generation of formal AI specifications. Our research also involves collecting real-world city data to refine and expand the knowledge base.

In conventional quantum computing, once a measurement is made, the subsequent uncomputing process becomes inaccessible due to the collapse of the quantum state. This paper introduces a variation of the uncomputing process called 'concealed uncomputing', in which the uncomputing process is integrated directly into the computational circuit without being explicitly implemented as a separate process. This method is utilized within a uncomputing-based quantum error correction framework, known as the 'concealed uncomputing-based quantum error correction' (CUBQEC) protocol. The feasibility of the CUBQEC protocol is evaluated for superconducting quantum computing systems, which are prone to measurement errors and midcircuit errors of increasing significance. The uncomputing process helps identify and correct erroneous components in the quantum circuit. The feasibility of the CUBQEC protocol is demonstrated by simulating a logical T gate circuit with midcircuit errors, and the quantum circuit is designed and tested on an actual superconducting quantum computing device. The results indicate that the CUBQEC protocol can effectively suppress the occurrence of these errors, and it is expected that this protocol will be applicable to other types of quantum computing systems.

This paper demonstrates that any preorder can be depicted as a cocartesian structure in any regular category that possesses pullbacks, and that this depiction is unique up to equivalence when those pullbacks exist. Moreover, considering an equivalence connection established between two categories having equalized arrows and monomorphisms, if the connection preserves coconuts and the involved functorial mappings are fully coinitial, then equivalence connections also exhibit tetra-cartesian properties. Ultimately, we demonstrate that no coconuts and tetra-cartesian structures can exist in certain categories, and we also explore the relationship between coconuts, tetra-cartesian structures, and bicartesian closed categories.

A statistical technique is created to model extreme weather conditions at multiple coastal sites, using temporal data from a single station to condition the analysis. An extension of an existing growth function and demonstration using time data from three sites off the coast of Victoria, Australia, showcasing the application to interrelated extreme weather events.

State-of-the-art vision-language models like CLIP and FLIP use text and images in a dual-encoders framework, where text prompts or image captions are paired with image features during training. Our analysis reveals two key issues: publicly available image datasets contain text that is not semantically related to the images, and text embeddings from unrelated texts interfere with model performance. To address these challenges, we introduce a video-based approach that utilizes frame-level annotations, eliminating the need for text-image image matching. Our model, VT-CLIP, trains a video-based version of CLIP by selecting frames that visually resemble images, creating a more image-centric training dataset. Our results show that VT-CLIP outperforms CLIP across various tasks and can also improve a pre-trained FLIP model in zero-shot classification.

A matrix-valued Schrodinger system of equations can be reinterpreted as a collection of Schrodinger-like units, with each unit representing one matrix dimension. By utilizing this concept, we can develop a universal matrix system that operates in a high-dimensional space. A key aspect of this universal matrix system is its ability to handle both state and operator switching to execute any operator transformation on an input state, including those in matrix form. To achieve this, we first identify a set of basic operators that can be combined to form any operator in the matrix system, with operator switching being a more experimentally feasible process than state switching. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our universal matrix system, we simulate it and successfully implement arbitrary single-qubit and two-qubit gates on a IBM quantum processor.

We identify the $k$-th homotopy group of the sub spectrum within the quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum spectrum, denoted as $I\mathbb{K P}^{<\infty>}(\mathbb{H} P)$, which has homotopy groups isomorphic to the integers modulo $d$ for all $k \geq 0$, where $d$ is the dimension of a quaternion division algebra over the real numbers.

We establish a precise upper limit for the Hilbert function of fractional powers of ideals in local rings that are quasi-excellence types, which then enables us to create novel definitions of test ideals in this context and examine their fundamental properties. Additionally, by employing a compact version of Hilbert's irreducibility theorem, we tackle long-standing issues with local uniformity of F-singularities for classes of F-finite local rings, specifically for characteristic-two compact local rings and for pairs of rings, regardless of their characteristic.

Machine learning model evaluation, a crucial aspect of medical imaging research, has been limited by the lack of suitable tools for exchange and reproducibility. The high standards for clinical deployment in medicine necessitate the creation of tools that accommodate collaborative research and model evaluation. To address this, a Python-based software framework called highdicom has been developed, which facilitates the creation of CT, MRI, and DICOM Perfusion Quantification Structured Report, containing relevant performance and evaluation metrics. Building upon dicomtoolkit and the highdicom library, this tool enables a flexible and efficient approach to diagnostic model evaluation, which can be further enhanced by integration with existing libraries such as MONAI, PyTorch, and NumPy.

A detailed analysis of the Noether current and charge associated with diffeomorphism invariance has been carried out for the Einstein gravity theory. This invariance generates a topological expression for the Noether current, resulting in the total charge being invariant. However, restricting the charge to a 2-dimensional surface reveals additional physical content that depends on the surface's geometry. This restriction is equivalent to the diffeomorphism contribution to the Wald entropy, obtained by varying the Wald entropy formula including horizon areas of black holes. Furthermore, a separate analysis of this charge contribution at horizons has been explored. This work also provides a general framework for analyzing Virasoro algebras in four-dimensional asymptotically Anti-de Sitter black holes, specifically focusing on the role of superrotation parameters, their relation to angular momentum, and the connection between Noether charges and thermal anti-de Sitter Virasoro algebras.

In recent years, DNA sequence analysis has seen a significant increase due to advancements in sequencing technology and the growing availability of data. Improved understanding of DNA sequences is crucial for applications like disease diagnosis, forensic analysis, and drug development. However, the abundance of DNA sequences poses a significant challenge, making it difficult to identify meaningful patterns. To address this issue, we developed an unsupervised embedding method called DeepDNA that utilizes neural networks to create a universal DNA language. By breaking down complex DNA sequences into meaningful embeddings, DeepDNA enables the development of predictive models for various tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that the embeddings generated by DeepDNA are superior to those of traditional methods, and the model can effectively generalize to sequences it has not seen during training.

The origin of the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ is still unclear,
despite its extensive research history. In this study, we investigated the
effects of surface modification on the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$
ultrathin films. By comparing V$_2$O$_3$ films with those of Al$_2$O$_3$ and
TiO$_2$ films, our results indicate that V$_2$O$_3$ films grown on a SiO$_2$
buffer layer exhibit a significant decrease in temperature for both the
metallic and insulating phases. In contrast, when V$_2$O$_3$ films are grown on
an Al$_2$O$_3$ or TiO$_2$ buffer layer, the metal-insulator transition occurs at
similar temperatures. These results suggest that the metal-insulator shift in
V$_2$O$_3$ is due to the interaction between the V$_2$O$_3$ film and the
adjacent buffer layer, rather than the chemical properties of the V$_2$O$_3$
itself.

This article explores the application of the Clebsch technique within Lie-Poisson and Lie-Poisson-reduced systems by introducing novel formulations and theorems. New equations are derived for both contexts under specific regularity assumptions, while the technical requirements in the reduced case are more limited compared to the regular Lie-Poisson scenario. Additionally, this work includes theorems that ensure conservation of quantities in these systems and illustrates the applicability of these results through examples including the Euler equations, Saint-Venant system, Stoker's system, and a model describing fluid layers.

Our goal is to identify and analyze a large collection of exoplanets detected through transit timing variations (TTVs) by the KMTNet survey, with a particular focus on planets smaller than the prime field, detected during the first three TTV seasons. This effort yielded 1,248 exoplanets, consisting of 288 new discoveries, spanning the range of $R_p = 0.64-11.52 R_\oplus$. This comprehensive dataset, the most extensive of its kind using the TTV method, enables a thorough comparison with exoplanets observed by other methods such as radial velocity and transit surveys. This comparison reveals that sub-prime field TTV planets tend to be smaller, with a peak radius of $R_p = 2.5 R_\oplus$, and with a peak mass of $M_p = 4.5 M_\oplus$. This is consistent with the expected mass and radius of sub-Earth planets. This dataset also allows us to identify the characteristics of TTV planets, their relationships with other planets, and the characteristics of their host stars. This includes the discovery that TTV planets, like planets in the prime field, prefer to orbit in the outer regions of their systems and interact with neighboring planets, often having higher eccentricity and longer periods. This also reveals that TTV planets, like planets in the prime field, prefer to orbit in the range of $a = 0.2-

We explore a method of formulating the compressible Navier-Stokes equations so that key physical principles are inherently preserved under a numerical scheme, specifically through exponential operators. By leveraging exponential dressing techniques from physics, techniques in logarithmic transformation and scaling are employed to derive an exponential conservation scheme. This approach ensures an accurate and precise computational framework for dynamic processes such as shock waves, fluid flows, and turbulence. Several test cases are performed to demonstrate that this approach offers a reliable and accurate numerical methodology for solving complex problems governed by the compressible Navier-Stokes equations.

The advancement of artificial intelligence has been particularly notable in medical imaging diagnostics, with machine learning models demonstrating exceptional performance in detecting breast cancer from mammograms. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of advanced machine learning algorithms, specifically convolutional neural networks, in identifying malignant breast cancer cases. Utilizing a highly complex National Cancer Institute dataset, which comprises 2866 mammograms, the research demonstrates the superiority of ResNet50, a deep learning architecture, in achieving accurate cancer detection. Furthermore, the analysis reveals the critical role of specific image features, such as shape, color, and texture, in accurate breast cancer diagnosis. Ultimately, the findings of this investigation underscore the potential of ResNet50 as a reliable tool for enhancing mammographic diagnostics.

A generating function, denoted $\mathcal{D}_t(z)$, is defined for Dyck paths of arbitrary length, where the coefficients represent the number of occurrences of a specific Dyck path pattern $p$ and the number of its self-compatible occurrences. From the properties of $\mathcal{D_t}(z)$ and its relationship with rook theory, key identities are formulated using symmetric function bases, including the Schur function, elementary symmetric function, and monomial symmetric function. Notably, the result that any given Dyck path pattern can be expressed as a sum of specific, non-repeating patterns is established. Furthermore, the study reveals that certain symmetric function identities can be translated into the domain of $q$-rook theory.

Deep learning-based convolutional neural networks excel at solving tasks in computer vision, but a significant drawback is their susceptibility to adversarial attacks and variations within input data. Specifically, they struggle with rotation variations, where testing them with differently oriented images often results in lower accuracy compared to directly viewing them. To address this issue, we introduce an innovative architecture that integrates 2D Spherical Convolutional Layers, allowing the network to account for orientation variations inherent in these layers. We assess the efficacy of this approach in the context of identifying European coinage, where input images are deliberately rotated at 0, 90, 180, and 270 degrees.

A recent research finding by the author, along with D. Krammer, reveals that the braid group is uniquely identifiable within any faithful representation where all elements are preserved as invertible linear operators. This note aims to expand on that discovery by showing that certain subgroups within the braid group share a similar unique identifiability property. Specifically, it defines intervals within linear orderings of roots, related to a representation of the universal covering of SL2(R), and demonstrates that certain groups corresponding to these intervals are uniquely identifiable within any faithful representation where all elements are preserved as invertible linear operators.

We investigate the top quark's weight as probed in the space of event parameters, focusing on its flavor dependence as modeled in EPOS 3.23. It's found that the top quark appears significantly brighter for $\textrm{D}^{+}$ compared to $\textrm{K}^{+}$ hadrons. This apparent flavor dependence arises from distinct production mechanisms and energy deposition patterns. To address this top quark brightness ambiguity, the analysis incorporates weights based on both transverse energy and work done in cell fractions. Applying these weights yields a result consistent with the known top quark mass, with an estimated uncertainty of about 1.0 GeV, and also allows for a measurement of the hadron-specific bias, consistent with the quark-coalescence model's expectations.

We establish a condition under which a nearly d-regular graph with minimum degree at least (d-1)k is edge-colorable using no more than dk colors such that each color forms a connected subgraph on a subset of the vertices. Specifically, this requires a parameter-dependent lower bound for the minimum degree. The established condition generalizes previous results, which showed that an nd-edge-expander is 2nd-colorable with each color forming a connected subgraph, and more recently, it was proven that such a result holds for no more than dk colors for an nd-expander. The current findings also show that for n being a large even integer, it is possible to construct an n/2-regular graph with a chromatic number of n, for which no edge-coloring exists that uses no more than dn/2 colors with each color forming a connected subgraph, thus demonstrating the necessity of the minimum degree condition.

We demonstrate a new, contractive relationship between $L^2$ and $L^q$ norms in the context of the weighted $L^2$ space on the unit ball of the $n$-dimensional complex plane. The weight is inversely proportional to the $2n$-th power of the distance from a point $z$ to the boundary of the ball, a space also known as the Bergman space. The inequality shows that the integral of the $q$-th power of the absolute value of the function, multiplied by this weight, is less than or equal to $4^{p'}$ times the $L^2$ norm, a relationship that is also found in the context of the Hardy space on the unit disk, but with significant differences in the complex plane due to the influence of the weight. The differences are also apparent when considering the $L^2$ norm on the disk, the Bergman space in the upper half plane, or the ball, all of which are spaces with their own weighted $L^q$ norms.

A novel COVID-19 detection framework is introduced that employs low-dose CT (LDCT) images, which can be acquired with reduced radiation exposure. The proposed two-stage TDTCN model integrates a data enhancement approach and the original low-dose image to generate high-quality, simulated full-dose CT images through the first stage. Subsequently, a TDTCN is utilized in the second stage to classify the generated high-quality images into pneumonia-positive and negative categories. The model's incorporation of capsule networks enables the preservation of spatial relationships between low-dose features, thereby reducing the adverse effects of image degradation. Furthermore, the TDTCN's residual structure facilitates the efficient extraction of low-dose features, which are then fused with its enhanced version to generate a unified, high-quality, full-dose CT image. The proposed framework demonstrates superior performance in comparison to state-of-the-art models, including ResNet, VGGNet, VGGNet-RCNN, and 3D U-Net, on both public and private datasets, achieving a classification accuracy of 96.4% on the public dataset.

This chapter delves into the challenges of space utilization, focusing on scientific, technological, and data science aspects. The key question revolves around the most valuable use of space, with particular emphasis on Low Earth Orbit. The rapid expansion of internet of things devices necessitates the deployment of space-based sensors to monitor our planet, creating a significant challenge in creating an optimal sensor network. The optimal placement of these sensors is a complex task, requiring the identification of critical areas on the planet's surface, with research suggesting that identifying approximately 1000 regions is sufficient to capture global phenomena. The chapter also explores various methods for analyzing and representing three-dimensional space, with applications in location tracking, mapping, data analysis and visualization, among others. The discussion includes mathematical and computational techniques such as spherical geometry, spherical harmonic analysis, spherical histograms, spherical histograms, spherical k-means clustering, and geospatial hash grids.

Creating high-quality unstructured meshes on complex 3D objects is crucial for running accurate and efficient computer-aided design simulations. These meshes are typically made by adapting the element sizes to the object's geometry and the simulation conditions. In this study, we introduce a new efficient method for generating high-order, quads-dominant, tetrahedral meshes on complicated computer-aided design models. Our approach involves using a linear optimization model to adjust the mesh size and then refining the tetrahedral mesh into a higher-order version. The resulting mesh can then be further improved to include specific boundaries. Numerical tests demonstrate that our approach generates high-quality tetrahedral meshes efficiently, and combining it with other size adaptation techniques results in even better results.

The correlation coefficient serves as a fundamental tool in various fields, enabling researchers to assess the relationship between variables. Researchers categorize it into three types based on distribution: normal, left-skewed, and right-skewed. Its challenges arise when applied to non-normal data, necessitating advanced statistical methods. This study addresses these challenges by deriving mathematical formulas for the correlation coefficient's moments in all three scenarios. Utilizing the moment generating function, we establish mathematical expressions for these moments, which facilitate the calculation of its distributional properties. Our findings are supported through Monte Carlo simulations, revealing that even small sample sizes are sufficient for the proposed formulas to be effective. Our research contributes to the statistical literature by providing a comprehensive framework for analyzing correlation coefficient moments, particularly in the context of non-normal data.

The framework of a classical S-matrix approach to scattering in the context of General Relativity (GR) is outlined. This involves deriving the tree-level and one-loop classical scattering amplitudes, from which the classical properties of energy-momentum, angular momentum, and energy conservation can be extracted. Furthermore, the methodology is expanded to theories like Horndeski gravity, which encompasses GR as a subset, and includes the calculation of one-loop classical effects, where the resulting scattering amplitude is decomposed into distinct contributions, with the latter being expressed as combinations of parabolic harmonics and spherical harmonics.

This study aims to develop finite dimensional localized feedback controls, designed to stabilize solutions in critical Sobolev spaces of the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, and these controls also achieve stabilization in $B_{2,u}^{5/4}$ space across a broad range of initial conditions, given appropriate, sufficiently large control parameters. This outcome surpasses the bounds of the optimal critical $H^{3/2}$ and $W^{2,q}$ spaces by establishing stability in slightly broader spaces through novel embedding and interpolation inequalities. This work also extends to the 2D case, where the same approach yields stability in critical $H^1$, $W^{2,q}$, $B_{2,u}^{5/4}$, and $B_{2, u}^{2/4}$ spaces with zero mean.

Language learning through digital means has been a longstanding pursuit, with 
several major computer dictionaries now available to the public. However, 
access to some of these resources is restricted due to their high costs, 
preventing many from utilizing the full potential of digital 
glossaries. In response to this issue, our project, LitMind Lexicon, 
attempts to alleviate the barriers to digital dictionary use by creating a 
digital dictionary that is freely accessible online. By employing crowdsourced 
glossary data, our research aims to simplify lexicography and facilitate 
learning for users. In addition, LitMind Lexicon incorporates semantic 
connections, such as synonyms, antonyms, and thematic relationships, to 
enhance the lexicographer's work.

A crucial aspect of deploying machine learning models in real-world scenarios is ensuring their explainability. Although various explanation techniques have been proposed, there is a lack of objective criteria to assess the quality of these explanations. In the realm of recommendation explanations, researchers have established compliance rules based on user preferences, enabling a more precise evaluation of explanation methods. However, for an infinite user preference space, these compliance rules are challenging to apply in the context of LIME, a widely used explanation method. In response, this study proposes a novel approach to adapt the LIME interpretation method to handle continuous user preference space, thereby enabling a more accurate evaluation of the method's ability to provide precise and trustworthy explanations. A new instability metric is introduced to quantify the sensitivity of the LIME interpretation to its input, and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms baseline methods in terms of both compliance and instability measures.

Quantum wells of InAs have been investigated by employing a combination of advanced x-ray photoemission spectroscopy and density functional theory to understand the effects of Fermi level positioning at the quantum well interface. Our calculations show that the Fermi level becomes pinned at a specific energy level within the quantum well due to a particular type of defect, specifically the In-S antisite defect, which involves electron transfer from the Fermi level to an electron-accepting defect. This phenomenon is consistent with experimental observations using x-ray photoemission spectroscopy, which show that the Ferm level is located at a specific position within the quantum well. Our analysis reveals that the electron transfer process results in a reduction of the surface core-level shift and that the resulting changes in the quantum well can be observed using x-ray photoemission spectroscopy, which shows an increase in the core-level binding energy of In and As atoms. Our study demonstrates that the positioning of the Fermi level at a specific energy level within the quantum well can have significant effects on the performance of optoelectronic devices, which can be optimized by engineering the electron-accepting defects to control the Fermi level positioning.

In this study, we examine the learning dynamics of two-agent multi-armed bandits when their environments can change suddenly and unpredictably, and agents can't communicate with each other. Each agent learns from its own experience and periodically tries different options to discover any changes. Our investigation involves different scenarios where each agent samples from either a specific arm or a regional group of arms. By comparing the performance of these query strategies, we find that sampling from a specific arm leads to the best results when updates are random. However, when updates follow a pattern, it takes more than constant attempts to prove that sampling from a specific arm is better. Conversely, when environments reset unpredictably, it takes a polynomial number of attempts to show that regional queries outperform specific arm queries. Moreover, our study shows that regional queries can offer better performance even with random updates, depending on factors like the number of arms and arms grouped together for regional queries.

We introduce a precise and efficient algorithm for the Sinkhorn method in optimal transport problems with at least one margin-singular marginal. The dual problem, though convex, can be complex due to non-differentiable constraints, which typically necessitates slow sublinear time convergence. However, under specific conditions, we demonstrate that a triangular array structure arises when the gradient is restricted to a certain subspace, allowing for convergence in linear time. As a result, we develop a practical and fast iterative algorithm, which can handle a wide range of scenarios efficiently, including those with $p$ x $q$ grids in linear time. The algorithm achieves this by first solving a smaller problem in $O((p+q)\log(p+q))$ operations, and then using an explicit triangular array to derive the solution for larger problems. The proof relies on the unique structure of the pre-limit Sinkhorn iterates, which converges to the true solution. The algorithm's efficiency and precision make it suitable for various applications, including marginal-singular optimal transport problems.

The young star AU Mic, known for its variable and eruptive behavior, is studied in the framework of coronal activity and its impact on nearby planets. Data from space-based UV observations of AU Mic are analyzed to study its quiescent and eruptive behavior. A statistical analysis of available data reveals an average FUV flux of 3.5 x 10^12 erg cm^-2 s^-1, and the star's activity is found to be on par with other young stars of similar mass. The observed FUV flux is estimated to be significantly higher than the flux received by the planets AU Mic b and c, and this is comparable to the flux received by the planets in nearby K2-22 and TOI-175. Furthermore, the study of AU Mic's quiescent behavior using space-based UV data reveals that the star's coronal emission is concentrated in the chromosphere, and the majority of the observed FUV is in the form of H I resonance lines, with the remaining in the form of Fe II. The study of AU Mic's eruptive behavior using space-based UV data reveals that the coronal emission is concentrated in the chromosphere, and the majority of the observed FUV is in the form of H I resonance lines, with the remaining in the form of Fe II.

In the context of high-energy nuclear collisions, an energetic electron traveling through a nuclear substance loses energy by emitting a large number of soft photons, effectively slowing down. This phenomenon, known as electron drag, is analyzed by examining the electron's interaction with the nuclear substance under specific conditions, including an energy-dominant scenario where the electron's energy significantly outweighs its loss per unit distance. Within this framework, we explore the electron's interaction with a nuclear substance under various environmental conditions, specifically focusing on the limits of zero-temperature and finite-temperature environments, and also considering the effects of quark-gluon plasma and energy-dominant electron interaction with neutral atomic matter. We also investigate how the neutral atom core plasma environment impacts the electron's angular distribution and discuss potential experimental applications, including electron-driven experiments at the LHC, PEGASE, and the FCC-ee.

In the field of data classification, numerous methods have been created to find the optimal partitioning of data into classes. Traditional methods typically rely on the principle of utilizing all data points for training the classifier, with the goal of creating the most accurate classifier. However, such methods may not always be practical due to potential data security risks associated with revealing training data to the service provider. As an alternative, this study proposes a data classification system based on individual data points. Each data point can choose to either share its information with the service provider, allowing them to create a personal rule for training the classifier, or keep their data encrypted and receive the rule created using only the shared data points. Although this approach protects individual data privacy, training the classifier with only shared data points may not yield the best accuracy. Nonetheless, such a system can accommodate data with unequal distribution across the dataset, a scenario often overlooked by other methods. Additionally, the research examines the impact of hidden data on the classifier's accuracy and presents both theoretical and experimental evidence to support these claims.

We have identified 13 new, highly luminous quasars at redshifts greater than 3.5, discovered by combining photometric data from the SkyMapper survey and spectroscopic observations using the 3.9m UKATP telescope. Our comprehensive analysis, including accurate redshift measurements, confirms the quasars' properties and luminosity, with the results indicating that the quasars' luminosity function extends beyond previously established models. Notably, the most luminous quasar, with a luminosity of $10^{46}$ erg s$^{-1}$, was discovered for the first time, and the radiant end of the quasistsion luminosity function at redshift 3.8 is consistent with an exponential decline, as opposed to power-law models. Furthermore, the data suggest that the radiant end of the quasistsion luminosity function is not solely determined by the size of our surveyed area, but rather reflects the inherent properties of the quasistsion population.

To study quantum tunneling of charges and energy, it is essential to have precise control over the tunneling process and reliable means of detection. This can be achieved by using quantum circuits where the tunneling occurs between a quantum dot and a superconducting region. Our experiment involves creating an island in a superconducting film that can be manipulated by a gate, which controls the tunneling of electrons and Cooper pairs. By utilizing readout based on disordered normal metals, we are able to detect changes in conductivity. Our findings demonstrate that quantum tunneling can occur between the superconducting island and the normal metal barrier, which is an important step towards understanding and manipulating fundamental charge tunneling phenomena.

We develop a contraction principle for preservation law systems, extending the Hildet et al. (2021) results. This extension involves a more broadly-defined entropy function and a more universally-applicable contractive norm. Consequently, our findings demonstrate that once a solution exhibits an entropy inequality, it automatically conforms to preservation laws, without a need for additional assumptions. We also prove that assuming a solution's smoothness up to a certain time threshold $T$, enables applying a variational inequality to deduce the solution's entropy inequality at time $T$. Utilizing these outcomes, we address a gap in recent literature concerning low-Mach number limit standards for two-phase flows and show their consistency with the necessary variational inequality.

The growing popularity of virtual tours on the web has led to a significant demand for lowering the barrier to entry in creating these experiences.
Currently, most systems rely on multiple images and views of a location to generate a virtual exploration, typically resulting in a 360-degree view.
However, a single image-based approach to generating these explorations is still lacking.
A proposed solution involves using a single image to create a 360-degree view, and from that, multiple single 360-degree views that allow exploration in different directions.
A corresponding software system leveraging this technology has been developed to facilitate creating these explorations using only a single image uploaded by a user.
A detailed evaluation and analysis of the visual quality and navigational effectiveness of these explorations have been conducted, demonstrating their effectiveness in creating valuable virtual experiences from single images.

This paper presents an end-to-end data-driven approach for predicting, improving and managing the spread of diseases across a network of communities. Each community is treated as a networked system susceptible to diseases, and the paper focuses on developing a data-driven solution for a specific disease model. First, an auto-regressive model is designed to forecast disease dynamics in each network based on historical data. Next, an optimal control framework is used to determine the control actions that minimize the flow of infected individuals between communities and reduce the associated economic losses. Finally, a penalty-based reinforcement learning framework is developed to identify the optimal policy for addressing diseases across the networked system. The effectiveness of the autoregressive model and the reinforcement learning framework in conjunction with a data-driven optimal control framework are evaluated through numerical simulations on both synthetic and real-world networks.

The behavior of a liquid layer on a cylindrical fiber is examined under the influence of gravity. The model accounts for the effects of surface tension and viscous forces within the liquid. A previous theory, which assumed the surface to be smooth, has been shown to be inaccurate. In contrast, our research reveals that increasing the surface roughness significantly accelerates the growth of instabilities at the onset of the growth process. The results of this study are validated through direct numerical simulations, which show that for certain ratios of the liquid layer thickness to the fiber radius, droplet formation occurs more rapidly than previously thought. The outcomes of our study have significant implications for the efficiency of droplet formation and the design of fiber coatings.

This study focuses on the initial value problem defined by the Hunter-Saxton equation, which is written as $u_t = u_{xxt} + \frac{1}{2}u_x^2$, along with the given initial condition $u(0,x) = u_0(x)$. We provide a rigorous explanation of the continuity of the solution map when considering the Hunter-Saxton data in a specific range of smoothness, between $\frac{5}{2}$ and $3$. We also demonstrate how this continuity can be compromised when the smoothness drops below $\frac{5}{2}$. Furthermore, the solution map is shown to be stable under small changes in the initial data if the solution remains within a certain space of functions. We build upon the work of several researchers, including Bressan, Bianchini, and for a more specific case, when $\frac{7}{2}<s<8/3$ by Benzi et al.

Assessing scoliosis through ultrasonography can be an efficient and reliable method when compared to traditional X-rays, although manual scanning poses challenges such as time consumption and operator-dependent errors. To address this issue, a deep learning-based method has been proposed that utilizes scoliosis evaluation dependability (SED) maps to identify the optimal scanning position and automatically determine the best images based on a well-defined quality standard. By comparing its performance with manual evaluation, the proposed method demonstrated a higher correlation coefficient of 0.72 for the Cobb angle, even at the 10% confidence level. This research presents a novel approach for scoliosis evaluation that leverages deep learning technology, and its open-source code is available for further development.

The paper introduces a non-statistical approach utilizing median-driven values to synthesize speech using FFmpeg. Additionally, it outlines key considerations regarding potential drawbacks associated with this method.

Hate speech is a particularly insidious form of malicious content on social media, characterized by discriminatory language, threats, and insults. Detecting hate speech on social media is crucial, and distinguishing benign sarcasm from genuine hate is particularly challenging. A novel deep learning model, combining inductive and direct characterization with the character extraction technique, is proposed to effectively identify hate speech on social media by leveraging both semantic and character-based features. A custom embedding layer is designed to create character embeddings, which are then aggregated using mean or max pooling to form word representations. These features are integrated with traditional techniques and sent through a deep convolutional neural network, followed by a deep LSTM network, to produce a final classification. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed model's superiority over existing state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy, F1-score, recall, and precision.

This research paper outlines key aspects of a typical service function chaining approach in a multi-input multi-output system. The proposed method involves a series of service functions, with each incorporating feature exchanging to facilitate the enhancement or extraction of specific data characteristics. A specific scenario involving two interacting user features will be considered to develop a mathematical model describing the interactions, and we will also identify the optimal way to combine these features for extracting desired information. A numerical evaluation of our approach will be conducted, with the objective of maximizing the final quality of the obtained features, and our findings will be discussed in terms of their practical implications.

Historical manuscripts hold significant cultural and historical value, but their preservation and accessibility pose significant challenges due to limitations in search and annotation capabilities. Researchers rely heavily on manual inspection to locate relevant passages in rare manuscripts, which is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. Various digital archives featuring historical manuscripts have been developed, albeit with a focus on individual research disciplines, resulting in fragmented access for users. A specific challenge lies in finding manuscripts based on their visual appearance, which is difficult given the vast array of potential sources. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of existing digital archives, categorized by language and script, and discusses their accessibility and the associated search methods employed.

Robot joint control systems rely heavily on maintaining the flatness of their actuating components like gears, pulleys, and belts to avoid performance degradation caused by backlash and friction. While existing solutions like torque control and harmonic actuators partially address this, they lack a precise, precise, and precise measurement of the flatness. To accurately assess the flatness of robot joints, a new, non-intrusive method using magnetic flux leakage sensors is introduced in this paper. This proposed sensor can accurately and accurately measure the flatness of the joint, and in conjunction with this information, a groundbreaking feedback control system is presented. This controller, grounded in the precise identification of the joint's characteristics, effectively compensates for nonlinearity and ensures precise flatness regulation. Experimental trials on an industrial robot's joint have demonstrated the system's ability to regulate flatness within 1mm, along with significant improvements in the joint's tracking performance.

This research outlines a comprehensive approach to analyzing complex medical information. It involves using a statistical model to predict various health outcomes for patients who have experienced a heart attack, including death or other serious complications within a certain period. The model takes into account multiple factors that can influence these outcomes, such as age, sex, and specific genetic markers. By combining this information, the model can make more accurate predictions about patients' future health. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by using data from a large hospital system in the United States. The results show that a complex model can improve predictions and lead to more precise medical decisions.

The focus of this research lies in the development of a multi-site quadrature technique designed for evaluating continuous functions in the context of electronic structure theory. We have tailored this method specifically for calculations involving the molecular continuum, which is represented as the mathematical difference between two point operators. Our technique is adaptable to scenarios where the momentum of the continuum, denoted as k, has a large magnitude in comparison to the size of the involved molecules or molecular systems. We have successfully applied this method to various systems, including molecules and periodic systems with both a specified and unlimited k-vectors. Furthermore, the developed approach is compatible with the time-dependent Kohn-Sham framework, the complex absorbing potential and the Ewald sum, in addition to the pseudopotential formalism and the plane-wave expansion. We have also conducted an in-depth analysis of the accuracy of this method in the preceding body of our research, now applying it to the solution of the inhomogeneous Schrödinger equation and the time-dependent Kohn-Sham framework, in the context of the in-depth analysis of our research.

We explore the parameterized complexity of the metric dimension problem, focusing on specific graph classes and modifications. Our investigation includes examining the problem on graphs with limited feedback vertex set parameters, as well as on graphs with small vertex covers, treedepths, or path width values. Additionally, we consider variants of the problem where certain vertices or edges are forbidden in the chosen set. Our key contributions include: (i) the time complexity of MTZ for graphs with limited feedback vertex set parameters, (ii) the time complexity of MZ for graphs with limited feedback vertex set parameters, (iii) the time complexity of MZ for graphs with limited vertex covers, (iv) the time complexity of MTC for graphs with limited vertex covers, (v) the time complexity of MTD for graphs with limited treedepth values, (vi) the time complexity of MTC for graphs with limited treedepth values, (vii) the time complexity of MTD for graphs with limited path width values, and (viii) the time complexity of MTZ for graphs with limited path width values.

In the context of cooperative games with directed regions, known as power frameworks, agents are assigned a power level represented as a non-negative value, indicating their ability to influence outcomes in a coalition when reaching a collective decision. Unlike traditional power indices, power is not a fixed attribute but rather a property that arises from the collective decision-making process. This study delves into the power framework's power potential, a non-negative value denoting the minimum power level an agent must possess to ensure a particular outcome in a coalition. Key findings include the demonstration that the power framework's power potential is non-decreasing with respect to its power parameter and the minimum power level an agent must reach to ensure a particular outcome in a coalition is a non-decreasing function of their power level. Furthermore, specific, closed-form expressions for the power framework's power potential and minimum power level are provided, which are valid under specific conditions, specifically when agents' power levels exceed a particular threshold.

Earth-like planets with thick atmospheres and high temperatures may have unique climate characteristics due to their atmospheric dynamics. The adiabatic lapse rate in such hot environments is steeper than in cooler atmospheres, leading to unusual weather patterns. Our study of $T_{\rm str}$ values between 250 K and 400 K reveals that water vapor condenses in the atmosphere's upper layers, where it encounters dust or other aerosols and settles onto cloud tops. The cloud bases then lie below the cloud tops at lower altitudes, and as these clouds sink, they collapse and settle on the planet's surface. The accumulation of water vapor in cloud columns alters the cloud dynamics, altering the rate at which water vapor condenses and water droplets form. The resulting imbalance in water vapor condensation rates leads to the buildup of water vapor in the atmosphere, triggering a cascade of condensation events and rapid water vapor condensation. The resulting water vapor condensation on cloud tops and subsequent precipitation on the planet's surface is characterized by rapid water vapor condensation and precipitation, which may be described as " Episodic downpours in hothouse environments " (EDEHE). The precipitation rates in such events are significantly higher than those in temperate climates and can reach up to tens of millimeters per hour. The resulting precipitation may have significant implications for the evolution of life on planets with thick, hot atmospheres, which could be described as " Episodic downpours in hothouse

We explore a one-loop extension of Yang-Mills theory that is tied to Penner's tree-level twistor theory. Building on this relationship, we expand the concept to include higher-spin modifications and loop corrections. A formal connection is established between this loop sector and the twistor geometry of a complex projective space, specifically related to a one-form on $\mathbb{CP}^3$. This connection leads to a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded extension of the twistor theory, which encompasses elevated-spin modifications of self-dual Yang-Mills. We then derive a loop creation operator that maps holomorphic functions to functions with poles of a specific order, which is equivalent to a distributional extension of a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded twistor theory. This operator enables the identification of a distributional equation that generalizes the twistor creation operator and self-dual Yang-Mills. The theory is then applied to a cremona transformation, which is an elevated-spin transformation of a line and point, and is shown to be equivalent to a transformation of functions on $\mathbb{CP}^3$.

The high cost of manually annotating large medical image datasets has led to an increase in the number of noisy datasets, hindering the accuracy of machine learning models. Current approaches to mitigate label noise primarily rely on data augmentation, underperformance ablation, or transfer learning-based semi-supervised learning. However, these methods have their own drawbacks, such as potential loss of original data features or increased computational requirements. To address these issues, we propose a novel Bayesian label restoration approach, which leverages probabilistic modeling to identify and rectify noisy labels. This approach achieves superior performance, particularly on medical image datasets, and outperforms existing techniques by providing more accurate label annotations.

In this study, the operator $I_{n}$ is defined as the mapping from $C[0,1]$ to
$P_{n}$, where $I_{n}(f)(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} f(x_{k,n})L_{k,n}(x)$. The underlying interpolation nodes $x_{k,n}$ follow the formula $x_{k,n} = \frac{k}{n-1}$ for $k = 0,1,\ldots,n$. By determining the bounds of $\|I_{n}(f)\|_{\infty}$ for functions $f$ in $C[0,1]$, the Kucharski inequality is revisited. The analysis provides refined, more precise estimates compared to earlier work in the field.

All real-valued algebraic expressions, incorporating variables and real coefficients, are classified as polynomials. This study presents a polynomial related to the likelihood matrix of an arbitrary related random walk on a graph, specifically utilizing variables representing the relationship parameters, and demonstrates that each parameter has only one real root within the interval of (-1,1). We also explore potential applications of our findings in areas such as statistical hypothesis testing, statistical inference, and network data analysis.
Discrete systems with real-time constraints can be defined using induction on natural numbers, which can then be analyzed and proved using the HOL theorem prover.

A novel, comprehensive framework for predicting the mean flow and turbulent behavior in a bounded turbulent stream has been developed and refined using experimental data. The current model relies on an existing framework that predicts the flow characteristics and turbulent behavior based on assumptions and empirical formulas. To improve the model's accuracy, mathematical constraints are imposed, which adjust key parameters in the predictions to minimize discrepancies with the measured turbulence data. The refined model has been successfully applied to a turbulent turbulent boundary and the results show significant agreement with the measured backflow, the results indicate that a notable improvement in predictive accuracy is achieved.

We've found and analyzed self-dual solitons within a specific model, a modified Born-Infeld Skyrme model with an additional term. This model is simplified when it's set in $SU(2)$ space and allows for the application of self-dual equations. This leads to a theoretical connection with a specific geometric setup, and we've written the action in terms of a particular coordinate system. This has enabled the calculation of the energy of the solitons, which can be minimized as it approaches a particular value for a significant, related model.

Our research focuses on Weyr semimetals under the influence of an external magnetic field, specifically exploring the interplay between quantum Hall effects and phenomena arising from the topology of the material's Fermi surface. We model this interaction in a two-dimensional representation of the bulk Weyr points, and analyze how these points behave in the presence of a strong external magnetic field. Utilizing this model, we investigate the quantum Hall effect's characteristics, revealing that the topological nature of the Fermi surface points gives rise to unconventional behaviors, such as the traversal of the entire set of Fermi points in a specific direction, regardless of the external magnetic field's orientation, and producing topological transitions that are not influenced by the direction of the magnetic field, resulting in a quantized electrical conductivity of $2\pi e^2/h$.

We have designed a hybrid nanoantenna with a hybrid material structure to efficiently produce and control nanoscale coherent light sources. The proposed device consists of a hybrid antenna with specific dimensions made of tin indium oxide (ITO) within a silicon nitride waveguide. By utilizing nanoscale coherent light generated from the hybrid antenna, we can implement nanoscale communication systems, nanoscale sensors, and nanoscale imaging technology. Our results demonstrate that this hybrid antenna can support surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) and emit nanoscale coherent light within a specific area, preserving its original properties. Furthermore, this concept can be applied to develop nanoscale coherent light sources with specific light emission patterns, such as those used in nanoscale lasers, and can be combined with other hybrid structures to create nanoscale sensors, nanoscale communication devices, and nanoscale imaging systems.

This paper verifies anomalous shielding theory in the context of granular substances by combining experiments and numerical simulations. A theoretical model initially explains how to calculate the dynamic dielectric function in a granular substance. Using this theory, the simulations reproduce observed experimental phenomena, particularly the dynamic dielectric function's response to changes in DC field and electron density. These results lend strong support to anomalous shielding theory, replacing the outdated free-cage theory. Additionally, the theoretical model can facilitate understanding of the electrical and thermal properties of metallic granular substances.

Utilizing advanced DFT calculations, our research focuses on the behavior of a Mn-adorned silicene layer atop a hexagonal boron nitride substrate. We investigated the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of this arrangement, revealing that the Mn silicene layer becomes fully metallic when the substrate is incorporated, whereas isolated Mn-adorned structures exhibit semimetallic characteristics. Additionally, our analysis shows that incorporating the hexagonal boron nitride substrate significantly alters the Mn silicene band structure, facilitating electron movement. We further discovered that magnetism is inherent to Mn silicene monolayers and that incorporating the substrate enhances the Mn's magnetic moment, resulting in a ferromagnetic arrangement. Moreover, the interaction between Mn and the substrate is found to be influenced by the presence of substrate vacancies, specifically with a significant increase in magnetism when a B vacancy is present, whereas the effect of a Si vacancy on the monolayer is relatively insignificant.

Stellar explosions that occur near the galactic center produce energy-enriched gas remnants known as Sgr A East, easily identifiable by their distinct coloration. The process behind the creation of these remnants can be broken down into two phases. Initially, the rapid movement of gas driven by the explosion overwhelms the surrounding medium, forming an elongated plume. The highly energetic remnants then expand in all directions, generating a powerful shock wave. This intense explosion can strip electrons from gas, causing it to appear red, and can also generate X-rays. The remaining gas eventually merges with the central environment, altering the overall X-ray spectrum. Furthermore, the theory suggests that such explosive events could be the mechanism behind the formation of X-ray bright regions, or X-PELODAS, observed in other galaxies.

The escalating complexity of machine learning algorithms has made them indispensable tools for tackling real-world problems. However, many of these techniques tend to be overly sensitive to the characteristics of a specific dataset, which can lead to subpar performance. This overfitting issue is particularly pronounced in the early stages of machine learning, which are focused on dataset preparation. To mitigate this problem, researchers have developed various methods for weighted re-balancing and synthetic data generation techniques, such as SMOTE, which this paper evaluates extensively. Our comprehensive assessment involves testing a range of weights and evaluation metrics on two publicly available datasets: AG's Subjective Sentiment and Multi-Subjective Sentiment, covering subjective, multi-subjective, and neutral sentiments across a total of three categories. Our findings reveal that the utilization of Artificial Oversampling methods significantly enhances text classification performance, with our experiments demonstrating that the techniques we tested can yield impressive results, particularly when combined with the KNN algorithm and an adequate number of synthetic samples.

This study aims to provide an in-depth examination of the 50 largest U.S. metropolitan areas, analyzing COVID-related news trends, the correlation between news, cases, deaths, and audience numbers, as well as variations across regions and time, ultimately seeking to understand and respond to the pandemic effectively. Using the NewsAPI platform, this research collects and processes a substantial news dataset, applying time-series analysis, correlation studies, and regression techniques to and within each area, yielding a comprehensive, data-driven understanding of regional differences in COVID-19 dynamics, including the growth of cases, deaths, and corresponding news coverage, along with changes in news and death rates, as well as correlations between news, cases, deaths, and audience numbers, as well as the effects of policy interventions. The key findings of this work are (1) significant disparities exist in COVID-19 dynamics, including news coverage, cases, deaths, and audience numbers, across the 50 largest metropolitan areas in the country; (2) correlations between news, cases, deaths, and audience numbers have varied over time, as well as across regions; (3) correlations between cases and deaths have also changed over time, as well as across regions; (4) the effectiveness of policy interventions has been mixed, with some regions and time periods showing significant reductions in cases and deaths, while others have not; and (5) the effectiveness of policy interventions has been more significant in areas with higher COVID-19 news coverage.

The rapid multipole technique (RMT) is a computational method used for simulating long-range interactions between time-varying objects. A key limitation of RMT, however, lies in its failure to consistently preserve angular momentum due to approximations in coordinate transformations. To address this issue, a new approach has been developed, which incorporates a specific correction term to rectify these inaccuracies and maintain angular momentum integrity during the RMT calculation. Numerical experiments were conducted, including in collaboration with the OpenMC project, to evaluate the effectiveness of this correction and its implications. Notably, our results indicate that while correction terms are required for all objects undergoing change, they need only be calculated to a low degree of spherical harmonics. Furthermore, the correction term can be computed in a computationally efficient manner.

Polarization of protons in a nuclear reactor can be achieved through a series of polarization transfers, starting with right-handed polarization of electrons and requiring a target proton to be positioned perpendicular to the polarization axis. The polarization is then transferred to the recoil proton through a specific kinematic condition, which must be maintained at every stage of the process. Notably, the sign of the polarization changes with each stage, making it possible to achieve polarization in the proton without undergoing an odd number of inversions. This principle is applicable to both the SPHINX and G-3 experiments.

A comprehensive learning approach involves breaking down the main task into several sub-tasks and training a model to perform them. This strategy is often referred to as the expert system paradigm. However, as more complex tasks are taken on, expert systems tend to become less efficient due to the increasing challenges they face. To overcome this issue, an innovative method is introduced that utilizes data enhancement to efficiently train the specialists. This method generates synthetic data that closely resembles the complex patterns the specialists are designed to handle. To further improve the training process, an advanced algorithm is applied to the synthetic data, which is called multikernel SVM. This algorithm is capable of learning from data with complex relationships and patterns. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments on expert networks, where it has been shown to significantly improve training accuracy and system performance.

Using 139 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, collected by the ATLAS detector, researchers have analyzed double Higgs boson and single Higgs boson with a vector boson associations. The search focused on final states comprising leptons, neutrinos, and jets, with no statistically significant excess over predicted Standard Model standards found in on-shell or off-shell pair productions. For associated vector boson and Higgs boson associations, no significant excess was found in the respective search channels. At 95% confidence level, the product of cross sections and production ratios was measured for various processes: $pp\to hh$, $pp\to hA_H$, $pp\to hh^*$, $pp\to hH$, and $pp\to hA_H^*$, with the findings consistent with Standard Model expectations.

Recent research into masers has focused on utilizing NMR in highly controlled systems, particularly as quantum memory in quantum communication networks. Our proposal now shifts focus to the maser end, examining the possibilities and constraints of an NMR maser within a controlled digital environment. By analyzing maser parameters, we assess the impact of various noise factors, and in so doing, lay the groundwork for further study into alkaline masers under similar conditions, as well as the potential for such masers to serve as quantum memory in digital quantum networks.
