A neutralino has been suggested as a suitable dark matter candidate under the standard neutralino assumption. Nonetheless, a more comprehensive understanding of neutralinos is necessary to accurately model their properties. It is now proposed that a neutralino's evolution over time, due to a nonzero and decreasing self-annihilation cross section, could significantly impact the universe. This dynamic could lead to a power law expansion rate under specific conditions related to neutralino mass and energy density. Notably, a neutralino with a mass of 0.001 eV under these conditions can serve as a suitable dark matter candidate and generate a dark energy equivalent to the cosmological constant. As a result, such a neutralino can produce observable gamma radiation in the sky, with implications for further research.

The genus of a graph G, often referred to as its minimal genus, refers to the minimum number of handles required to embed G in 3-dimensional space without any self-intersections. Graphs are considered 3-connected when removing any single edge or vertex does not result in their disconnection. We present an novel algorithm capable of embedding a graph G in 3-dimensional space, where the number of handles is proportional to the square of the size of its larger endpoint, divided by the square root of the minimum degree, with a time complexity of O(n^4). This algorithm enables us to approximate the genus of thick graphs in polynomial time, with a precision of at least Ω(n^3).

In this research, we investigate a distributed convex optimization issue where multiple agents aim to minimize the total value of their respective convex cost functions. To address this challenge, we present a novel randomized Newton algorithm that employs each agent's local Hessian information to execute the method. This algorithm integrates random coordinate descent with a localized randomization technique to tackle the problem. Notably, it allows for the execution of second-order optimization methods without requiring the sharing of Hessian information among agents. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method converges to the optimal solution and achieves faster convergence rates compared to the distributed randomized linear optimization algorithm proposed by Beck and Teboulle. Furthermore, it surpasses a recently proposed distributed random block Newton algorithm in terms of the rate of convergence.

Social media platforms have become breeding grounds for harmful online behavior,
including harassment, bullying, and the spread of hate speech. The rapid growth
of the two major Indian languages, Hindi and Bengali, in terms of internet usage,
demands effective filtering systems for these languages on social media platforms.
To address this need, researchers have developed a dataset consisting of 50,000
labeled posts, 25,000 for each language, to train and test hate speech
detection models. Our study compares various cutting-edge deep learning models,
including RoBERTa-BERT, for hate speech classification in Hindi and Bengali
languages. The experiments revealed that RoBERTa pre-trained on Wikipedia
data from its respective language outperformed other models, with a remarkable
98.7% accuracy on clean datasets and impressive performance on data preprocessed
to remove emojis and handle special characters.

The challenge of identifying the recoil atom in direct electron capture experiments proves to be an insurmountable challenge, primarily due to the minuscule scale of recoil atoms. To address this problem, we have developed a state-of-the-art apparatus, the gas time projection chamber, capable of pinpointing the recoil atom. This device features four distinct operational parameters, which we have individually examined to optimize the detection process. Specifically, we have tailored our analysis around three of these parameters: the electric field configuration, the electron multipliers, and the data acquisition system. Furthermore, we have highlighted the critical role of the fourth parameter, the quenching gas, in ensuring the successful implementation of the recoil detector.

Driving a vehicle is a complex process that requires significant attention and focus.
Despite advancements in smart coaching technology, there is still a lack of widely accepted standards for monitoring and assessing driving behavior.
This study proposes a new system of smart coaching, utilizing machine learning algorithms to analyze and evaluate driving data from various technology providers.
Through the integration of these tools, the system provides drivers with timely feedback and assistance, allowing them to improve their driving skills and make more informed decisions.
Our research highlights the importance of considering diverse driving styles and preferences when developing smart coaching technologies.
Our study utilizes data from over 100,000 drivers across 10 different monitoring services, analyzing nearly 10,000,000 driving sessions.
Our results indicate that specialist moderation of machine outputs can lead to more accurate and fair assessments of driving behavior, ultimately contributing to the development of more equitable and effective smart coaching technologies.

This report details the results and evaluation metrics of the Out-of-Lexicon Challenge, an out-of-domain and out-of-vocabulary text classification task. The report tracks the out-of-competition tests across four tracks. The overall performance metrics, rankings, and detailed results for each team are presented, along with the evaluation criteria and frequency of the unique vocabulary used, which exceeded 500,000 words.

The structural complexity of various systems, including materials, is characterized by intricate Gaussian stochastic field configurations. These fields are studied in contexts like disordered media and metastable landscapes. Our study focuses on a specific type of pathway, known as a geodesic path, within these fields, allowing for exploration of intricate geometries like spheres and tori. The development of these pathways facilitates an examination of their properties in relation to intricate geometries and dynamic processes, including the analysis of energy landscapes on diverse manifold types and the modeling of field-driven particle motion in disordered media.

This film is a sequel to the 2019 paper by A. Gizzetti and R. Benzi, titled "Duration matters, occasionally," which explored how sudden changes in financial markets might be influenced by information gradually released. The concept of an information leak was employed, and a two-layer model was utilized to simulate the behavior of a market maker. A market maker's order book, which evolves based on randomly arriving and departing orders, was considered a fundamental building block. In a market with two competing news sources, one of which significantly impacts the price, the order book's properties were found to dictate whether an anticipated news release will result in a notable price movement. This phenomenon, exemplified by the occasionally fully-transitive percolation model, was found to persist in the limiting properties of the order book. Consequently, the probability of significant price movements following a anticipated news release can be predicted using analytical tools, and this phenomenon may be observable in actual financial markets.

Let M be a modular structure defined over the rational numbers, with a level l greater than 3, and let's consider the Dirichlet L-functions derived from M's weight, denoted as w(M,s), and its modular components, denoted as $L(M, s, \rho)$, where $\rho$ is an irreducible two-dimensional representation of a specific group. We aim to establish upper limits on special values of these L-functions at s equal to w(M, 0) + 1, 2, and 3 for all possible irreducible representations $\rho$. Furthermore, by applying the Taylor expansion principle for elliptic divisibility sequences and cross-referencing with our initial findings, we derive two significant consequences: first, the torsion points under a level M map from the genus 1 curve C are completely contained within the Weil restriction of the elliptic curve E, denated as $E_R$, and second, the torsion points under a weight 2 binary form f are contained within the Weil restriction of the corresponding ideal class group's ray class field.

We've found that by manipulating strain in the graphenew edge, we can control how spin and charge move through the graphenew edge, which has significant implications for spintronics. Our analysis using the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation revealed that deforming the edge shape can effectively modulate spin-sensitive, quantum-coherent transport and even produce tunable spin filters. The findings also show that by applying strain along the edge, we can control both spin and charge, which opens the door for potential applications in spintronics. The non-relativistic model we used is highly accurate and takes into account all relevant effects that arise from physical depositions, unlike previous semi-relativistic models.

Operator-correction techniques have recently been applied to establish operator correction theorems, which extend traditional approximation theorems in numerical analysis. This paper aims to develop operator correction theorems, particularly Korovkin type theorems, for both linear and nonlinear approximation theories. It presents operator correction theorems for mildly nonlinear, monotonic operators and approximating operators that are linear, nonlinear, positive, and monotonic. Specifically, this paper utilizes a new concept of mild nonlinearity introduced by the authors, along with the notion of a K-space. The paper's findings are illustrated by several numerical examples.

Given a pancyclic graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and minimum degree $\delta(G)$, we demonstrate that the graph's largest independent set has size at least $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{7\delta(G)-n}{4-\delta(G)}$, with the Hamiltonian nature allowing the bound to be further increased to at least $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{3\delta(G)-n}{4-3\delta(G)/2$.

This research investigates the movement of optical hadrons in various collision environments, including gold-gold collisions and isobar interactions at a 200 GeV energy level. By using the multi-component diffusion model, we examine the influence of different factors on optical hadron behavior. Notably, our analysis reveals that the hadron state in gold-gold collisions closely resembles that in proton-proton collisions, displaying similar characteristics. Notably, our results also indicate that the hadron distribution in gold-gold collisions is broader than that in proton-proton collisions.

The Spectral Koopman approach efficiently handles complex dynamical systems models using a small dataset and a specific kernel function. However, increasing system complexity or the dimensionality of states and controls leads to a significant rise in computational and memory requirements. To mitigate these challenges, we have developed a novel technique that integrates sparse-grid methods and an adaptive algorithm to dynamically adjust the data points' distribution. By doing so, the proposed method achieves a substantial reduction in computational burden and dimensionality without compromising accuracy, thus making it suitable for a broader range of applications. The effectiveness of this technique is demonstrated through the successful prediction of various systems, such as nonlinear systems, and high-dimensional linear systems like the 2D Navier-Stokes equations, and the application of model predictive control.

A new approach, referred to as the Outside Complicated Scaling (OCS) method, has been developed to analyze how wave functions of systems undergo scaling in the DC spectrum. This technique decouples the complex scaling operator, whose analytical form is impractical for most atoms and molecules, facilitating numerical investigation. A comparison with embedded complicated scaling (ECS) method reveals that OCS yields results with comparable accuracy at a significantly lower computational cost. A demonstration of OCS has been successfully performed for hydrogen atom and molecular ion $H_2^+$ under strong DC fields using configuration interaction method.

For a given Schrödinger kernel with Marginal constraints, the existence of transport plans is not guaranteed. Still, the convergence of the Sinkhorn algorithm is demonstrated for an increasing sequence of couplings satisfying the Marginal constraints, even when it does not converge to a transport plan fulfilling the Schrödinger kernel, under certain conditions. The Momm's Theorem is reformulated to accommodate this scenario. Furthermore, the rate of the Sinkhorn algorithm's divergence is quantified. This finding is illustrated with examples.

This study measures the cross-section of $t\text{-}\bar{t}$ creation at a 5.02 TeV proton-proton center-of-mass energy using the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis incorporates data collected in 2016 and 2017. The measurements account for two distinct final states: one with two opposite-sign top quarks and another with two top quarks having the same charge. The observed cross-sections are 6.9 and 0.79 picobarns respectively. The analysis also compares these measurements with a seven picobarn cross-section recorded at a higher energy of 7 TeV.

A key feature of complex systems lies in their modular structure, which is characterized by distinct components that interact with each other and influence one another. This study focuses on a system with a central module, where the central module is interconnected with multiple peripheral modules, and we examine the conditions under which a system's modularity becomes localized to the central module, especially when the modules are not equally sized. We develop a localization index to quantify the modularity index and analyze the effects of network size and connectivity on the system's modularity. We discovered that the modularity exhibits a localized phase transition when the peripheral modules are small and the conditions of localization are defined by the relative sizes of the peripheral modules and the connectivity within the central module. Furthermore, we found that the modularity exhibits power-law scaling when approaching a localized critical point, and we also observed localized hysteresis in the system's modularity.

This paper demonstrates that the generalizations of Bessel functions J_{nu}(z) and J_{nu}^{mu}(z) can be effectively categorized within the Janowski distortion series framework by applying suitable geometric constraints.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has significantly altered people's daily routines and social interactions worldwide. In this study, we analyzed the shifts in the daily movement patterns of the pandemic using data from 5,000 Beijing urban residents. By comparing pre-pandemic and pandemic periods, we observed notable changes in the average radii of circles of interaction (RoCs) and the frequency of interactions among individuals with different income levels. Notably, the pandemic caused a significant reduction in the average size of RoCs, with the effect being more pronounced for lower-income individuals. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that these changes led to a notable increase in income-based segregation, with the average clustering coefficient growing more significantly for lower-income individuals. This research focuses on the development of efficient numerical methods to solve two-phase flow equations in heterogeneous porous media using coupled nonlinear field-separated preconditioners. Building upon previous work, the authors extend the application of these preconditioners to porous media with varying permeability, demonstrating their capability to enhance convergence and accelerate solution times. Numerical experiments conducted on heterogeneous grids reveal that even slight variations in permeability significantly affect the distribution of pressure, relative permeability, and fractional flow. Notably, the proposed preconditioners show improved performance compared to standard Newton iteration, particularly when used in combination with multigrid methods.

We propose a novel design for a chiral optical device, which operates using a single polarizer and exhibits an asymmetric transmission pattern for both circular light components. The device's fundamental working principle is rooted in the phenomenon of non-Hermitian physics, which we implement in a passive configuration. Additionally, our analysis reveals that adding an active component to the system could lead to the creation of a non-reciprocal optical filter, which would be an essential element for a chemical or electronic light source operating on a chip, replacing bulky, traditional devices such as Faraday isolators.

Our research focuses on the connection between the 2D dilaton-black hole solution in Jackowski-Teitelboim JT gravity and a specific 4D semi-minimal, non-minimal conformal fixed point solution of the Liouville CFT, where the cosmological constant is set to zero. This particular Liouville CFT can be obtained through the compactification of a 4D gauge theory on a torus, and it has previously been shown that the thermal partition function for the JT gravity black hole matches the one-point function for the Liptser-Liouville CFT. By introducing the matrix framework, we have developed a geometric interpretation of the semi-minimal Liouville CFT, and in the process, the partition function for the JT gravity solution can be derived from the exact CFT result, thus establishing the JT gravity thermal partition function as the rescaled partition function of the Liouville CFT, and also confirming the CFT's bulk dual. This implies that the JT gravity black hole compactified on a circle has the same thermal properties as the Liouville CFT compactified on a torus, and the dilaton's zero mode in the bulk corresponds to the radius modulus of the torus.

This study utilizes the dp-coordinate system to find exact warp bubble solutions for an ideal fluid in the presence of a cosmological constant, $\Lambda$. Our results show that a balance between dark energy and spatial curvature is required to achieve a stable warp bubble. When these values are adjusted appropriately, the warp bubble can remain in a quasi-static equilibrium.

New York City's transportation infrastructure is monitored through numerous sensors, cameras, and devices, generating vast amounts of data. This data is crucial for analyzing the system's performance and enabling various applications such as traffic management, road maintenance, and transportation research. However, the vast scale of metropolitan areas poses significant challenges for data collection, processing, and analysis. To address these issues, the GUIDES framework proposes a unified approach to monitoring Metropolitan Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) by standardizing data exchange between sensors and applications. This paper outlines the research challenges and proposed resolution pathways for monitoring metropolitan areas within the GUIDES framework, including defining resolution standards for spatial data, temporal intervals, attribute sets, and error tolerance.

The dynamics of thermal equilibrium establishment among normal modes of temperature and their motion states can be studied through the application of a 2D ion lattice. Utilizing a laser cooling technique and a digital phase modulation method, we manipulate the 2D lattice and determine the temperature modes' equilibration time. By modulating the lateral motion with two possible methods - uniform heating and targeted mode heating, we observe the decay of a spin qubit's coherence as a response to these modulations. This allows us to derive key information about the system's thermal equilibrium, including its mode temperatures, motion state distributions, and thermal equilibrium speeds. Our results reveal a consistent and uniform mode temperature distribution, with each mode attaining thermal equilibrium at approximately room temperature, as well as a predicted model of thermal equilibrium based on the Coulomb crystal's damping mechanism.

A method with a comprehensive quantum approach is introduced to accurately evaluate the effects of chemistry and electromagnetism in TERS measurements. CHENEM is an in-depth method that simulates how the local electromagnetic field interacts with individual molecules at the surface, considering multiple interactions simultaneously. It is a rigorous quantum method that accounts for complex interactions between light and matter, unlike simpler quantum methods. Furthermore, CHENEM precisely calculates how the interaction affects both the interaction between molecules and the local electromagnetic field. To demonstrate CHENEM's effectiveness, it is applied to two scenarios: the interaction between adjacent ethylene molecules on a surface under specific conditions and the interaction between an ethyne molecule and a gold nanosphere when exposed to specific laser frequencies.

We investigated the Extragalactic Microwave Emission hypothesis by analyzing microwave emission in nearby galaxies. Using the Sardinia Radio Dish at 31.5 GHz, we observed 20 galaxies, including the Milky Way, and compared them to a control sample of 20 starry regions. Our precise measurements, made with a high angular resolution of 12 arcminutes, revealed no significant excess microwave emission in the selected galaxies. This absence of excess emission, along with our analysis, narrows down the total hydrogen content in the Milky Way to 5.3 to 6.3 times the disk's hydrogen content, providing the most restrictive limits yet. Furthermore, our comprehensive analysis, including modeling of the data, yielded the most stringent limits on the excess emission, including its color temperature and spectral index, and also set the most stringent limits on the fraction of hydrogen outside the disk, and its temperature.

Thermal properties of ammonium sulfate exhibit a significant entropy alteration that is linked to a significant negative thermal expansion, and this phenomenon is attributed to a reversible proton transfer. Research has revealed that the interaction between protons and oxygen molecules is characterized by a double-bond structure, consisting of a strong covalent bond and a weaker hydrogen bond. The incorporation of protons into a hydrogen bond causes a distortion of the oxygen structure, which in turn leads to a lengthening of the covalent bond, resulting in a notable decrease in entropy. Our computational analysis of ammonium sulfate has revealed that the variation in entropy is primarily a consequence of the substantial distortion of hydrogen bonds, which in turn affects the orientation of adjacent molecules.

In situations where the best possible outcome is unknown, humans and animals often learn through a process called reverse planning. This involves adjusting their learning based on the difference between the best possible outcomes and what they actually experience. This type of learning is thought to be a key part of brain function, as evidenced by neural activity in a brain region called the midbrain. 

We investigated how the limitations of memory affect this type of learning using a specific task and found that subjects' behavior was influenced by the limitations of memory, particularly when trying to identify the most valuable options. 

Using machine learning algorithms to simulate brain activity, we discovered that subjects' neural responses correlated with the specific prediction errors calculated based on limited memory. 

These results suggest that subjects' neural activity reflects an adaptive learning process that takes into account limitations of memory. 

This highlights the need to consider alternative learning mechanisms when studying brain function.

We propose a method for deriving the reduced exceptional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{l}_ {7, 25}$, which has 120 basis vectors and 120 weights, by reducing the 168 exceptional $E_8$ Lie algebra's properties. Our analysis of the weight structure of $\mathfrak{l}_ {75}$ employs an exceptional $E_8$ Lie algebra's exceptional properties. In a reduced root system, consisting of 108 roots and linked with the reduced weights, we explore contextuality and quantum entanglement. Specifically, an even number of roots can be arranged in pairs, where each root has a unique partner, and we consider a maximum set of 33 roots, where no three can form a triplet. Our work also identifies a maximum set of 26 weights, with no linear combination of three weights equal to zero.

In large-scale educational assessments, a significant challenge arises from the substantial amount of missing responses, which can severely compromise the accuracy of ability estimates. Conventional approaches, often applied item-by-item, neglect critical information regarding the interconnections between items and students, which can be leveraged to reduce measurement inaccuracies. This study introduces an innovative, iterative Bayesian method, capable of handling extensive missing data patterns commonly observed in contemporary large-scale assessments. Simulated assessment scenarios demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms the standard separate examination scoring method. Moreover, when tested on actual real-world assessment datasets, our method consistently yields enhanced performance, particularly when responses to easier and harder items exhibit substantial missing data.

A cutting-edge robot architecture, known as Interactable Robot Architecture (IARA), enables robots to collaborate and coexist in dynamic environments by allowing each robot to be aware of its peers and adjust its capabilities accordingly. IARA, grounded in Boids theory and Agent-Based Multi-Agent Systems, provides a framework for robots to establish temporary cooperative relationships, ultimately achieving shared goals through selective coordination of capabilities. This study presents a detailed analysis of IARA's foundations, along with a demonstration of a cooperative path-finding strategy, and offers a comparison with existing cooperative multi-robot systems, highlighting IARA's novel aspects and potential applications in autonomous robotics and game development.

Existing navigation systems are designed for environments they already know, which limits their application in new settings. To overcome this challenge, we've developed HitMap, a two-part hierarchical representation that enables robots to effectively transfer between unfamiliar environments. By combining a 2D topological map with a location map, HitMap facilitates navigation even when only part of an environment overlaps between the two. To test our model, we conducted extensive simulations on randomly generated environments and measured successful transfer rates. The results demonstrate HitMap's ability to transfer navigation skills with up to 90% effectiveness. Additionally, we applied HitMap to a real robot and demonstrated its capacity to transfer to unfamiliar environments without requiring a full map update.

As a potential solution for next-generation high-speed short-range communication, a spread-spectrum technique is being considered. The conventional short-range supplementary code sets typically rely on Zadoff-Chu (ZC) sequences and their two-dimensional counterparts, known as ZC-supplementary code sets. However, these methods have a drawback in that they introduce inter-group interference due to cross-correlation between different group sequences. To address this limitation, a novel, larger inter-group ZC-supplementary code set and its corresponding two-dimensional counterpart are presented, utilizing the properties of specific multivariable functions. The proposed code sets exhibit increased size compared to their conventional counterparts, and can be efficiently generated through a straightforward process. The effectiveness of the introduced code sets is supported by simulation results, and their potential applications are also discussed.

X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) enables the study of otherwise invisible internal structures. By using multiple energy levels, spectral CT can offer enhanced diagnostic capabilities, crucial for both medical and industrial applications. However, acquiring this type of data generates significant radiation exposure and substantial data storage requirements. Acquiring high-quality images while minimizing radiation dosage and data storage remains a significant challenge. Acquiring multiple scans to gather sufficient data for reconstruction leads to inaccurate results, particularly when data is sparse. To address these issues, a non-convex reconstruction framework utilizing dual total variation and block coordinate descent has been introduced. Initially, a joint reconstruction of two polyenergetic beamsets and sparsity of the material breakdown matrix are performed. Subsequently, a refined two-step process is performed to further minimize the cost function. The framework's effectiveness in both medical and industrial settings is demonstrated.

The optical properties of multi-layered nanostructures can be analyzed through the nonlocal hydrodynamic model, which is effective for structures with very small interlayer distances, typically under 1 nanometer. By assuming the electron density follows a step function, the nonlocal response can be derived for stacks of alternating metal and electron gas layers. In our study, we examine how the nonlocal hydrodynamic model impacts various phenomena, such as changes in reflectivity, shifts in resonance frequencies, and changes in mode sensitivity to layer thickness, layer spacing, and total electron density. We compare the results with those from the Drude model, taking into account the electron density and nonlocal effects, under the assumption that the electron density has a step function profile.

We examine the impact of a feedback mechanism on Contextual Named Entity Recovery, a subfield of Natural Language Understanding. This subfield focuses on reconstructing a named entity's internal structure based on its external context. In Collaborative Contextual Named Entity Recovery, users provide feedback in the form of importance weights for words, which helps improve the performance of the model. Our research investigates the role of this feedback loop for contextual named entity recovery. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of the state-of-the-art models and address an open question regarding the influence of user feedback on the reconstruction of a named entity. Our findings suggest that user feedback can lead to better results for short and medium-length entities, but not for all cases. We also reveal that the performance of the model is sensitive to the order in which examples are processed and suggest that user feedback may not be as effective for long entities. Furthermore, we observe that the performance of the model is influenced by the size of its training dataset and propose a novel architecture for deep neural networks that takes into account the specific properties of the recovery task, outperforming existing models.

The increasing use of screens has made it necessary to effectively manage the flow of sequential information. To accommodate the limited space on smaller devices, it is crucial to adapt to the space constraints. The conventional approach of displaying linear data or multi-dimensional time sequences in a linear format is not always suitable for sequences with multiple dimensions. A new dataset called MultiDimSeqs was created to present these sequences in a non-linear layout. However, users find it challenging to navigate the complex sequence structures. To address this issue, researchers have developed interactive techniques to facilitate navigation on MultiDimSeqs, using a dual system of horizontal and vertical zooming to enhance user experience.

This study introduces a novel method for predicting diverse clinical outcomes on a single patient using electronic health records, which is an underexplored challenge. Traditional classification models typically forecast a single label for a patient, whereas our approach treats the problem as a graph classification task, where each possible diagnosis or outcome is represented as a node in a graph. We propose a novel method to represent clinical conditions as a diverse diagnosis graph, incorporating various features such as ICD-10 codes, CPT codes, and patient demographics. Additionally, we use a new encoding scheme to handle the dynamic coding system and design a graph neural network to learn the diagnostic relationships and jointly predict multiple clinical outcomes. We conducted comprehensive experiments on two digital health datasets, demonstrating that our proposed model outperforms baseline methods and provides diverse, interpretable predictions.

This study explores the impact of a charged flexible polymer chain immersed in an electrolyte solution on the local electric field it generates using molecular dynamics simulations. Three levels of solvent polarization are considered: a fully polar solvent modelled with explicit water molecules, a continuum solvent modelled with the Poisson-Boltzmann equation, and a non-polar solvent that ignores any solvent polarization effects. It's discovered that taking into account solvent polarization significantly affects the local electric field and can even reverse its direction, an outcome that's more pronounced with higher surface charges and more rigid polymer chains. Additionally, solvent polarization significantly influences the counterion condensation phenomenon, resulting in a substantial increase in the fraction of counterions that condense onto the polymer chain.

Our approach involves a text processing pipeline that extracts software specification information from disorganized text sources. SoftSpecMiner, a component of our system, utilizes entity recognition to identify and extract software specification-related text from unorganized sources. We developed a comprehensive dataset of software specification text, consisting of 227 examples from 27 distinct software products, to train and evaluate our method. Experimental results demonstrate that SoftSpecMiner can accurately identify analogous entities within unbared text and adapt to classify them as software specification text or non-specification text in embedded contexts.

In a network of mobile devices, using a network encoding approach can greatly benefit applications such as the Internet of Things and mobile data centers by allowing multiple packets to be combined at both sender and relay nodes, thus reducing wireless traffic and saving bandwidth. To optimize this process and minimize energy consumption while avoiding packet collisions at shared medium relay nodes, a joint strategy is proposed, which involves joint determination of optimal relay schedules and power allocation for both sender and relay nodes. Two algorithms have been developed to achieve this: a non-linear algorithm and a linear approximation, yielding a joint strategy that achieves a specific level of optimality compared to the ideal solution. Extensive simulations confirm the efficacy and efficiency of the proposed joint strategy, demonstrating its ability to achieve specific performance gains in terms of energy consumption and traffic reduction, thus approaching the optimal performance of a specific baseline scheme and outperforming a specific state-of-the-art scheme.

Recent experiments have discovered that Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states occur in certain metal surfaces when a magnetic impurity is attached. These YSR states can potentially be utilized in spintronics due to their properties. A new theory, called Initial Principles Relativistic (IPR) theory, has been developed to study YSR states. This theory is an improvement over existing Kondo models, as it can be used with first-principles calculations to study ySR states in any material, rather than just specific types of materials. IPR theory can be used in a computational process to study the energy and other properties of YSR states in magnetic impurities and their interactions with metal surfaces. IPR theory has been tested using Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on Nb(110) surfaces, and the results closely match those of previous experiments. IPR theory can be used to study the effects of ySR states in spintronics devices.

This research introduces a method to reduce bias in transfer learning-based 3D object detection systems, which can inadvertently encode prejudices against certain object categories. Our approach consists of two stages: 1) An initial layer is modified to apply DNN filters, which use out-of-the-box statistics to dethrottle  network responses and minimize the risk of biased decision-making. 2) A DNN-based scan alignment method is developed to retrain the object detection model using a broader dataset, thereby mitigating the original bias. Our method's effectiveness and efficiency are validated through results on the Sun RGB-D dataset.

A novel method for satellite imagery edge recognition is introduced, where a machine learning classifier is trained to distinguish between edges and non-edges using basic image features. In contrast to deep learning methods, this approach boasts interpretability and training efficiency, along with the ability to leverage existing image processing techniques for optimal performance. Experimental results on various satellite image datasets, specifically the SpaceNet dataset, reveal that this method is on par with deep learning methods, achieving comparable mean intersection over union scores of 0.76 compared to the average of 0.78 for deep learning methods.

High-intensity X-ray laser beams enable the study of complex, non-linear dynamics occurring on a short timescale using near-edge electron groups dynamics. A new rate framework is proposed to analyze and predict non-linear processes involving these electron groups at a time when the x-ray field is strong. This theoretical framework accounts for x-ray intensity effects on core and valence electron dynamics, core ionization, and orbital relaxation, particularly in the context of saturation, and is demonstrated through an examination of Cu K-edge spectra under various regimes of x-ray intensity.

This paper presents the concept of Counterfactual Deep Neural Network Attacks and investigates their effects on deep learning-based Modulation Classification systems. Our study reveals that Counterfactual Attacks can be executed with relatively low success rates and can cause significant degradation of the target model's performance by altering only a few bits of the input data. As part of this research, a Real-time Deep Learning-based Automatic Modulation Classification system is developed and integrated with Software Defined Radio technology. Furthermore, a novel Counterfactual Attack method is proposed and evaluated, and our results show that such attacks can be launched even when the host model's weights are in an open state. To counter this vulnerability, an implementation of Adversarial Training defense method is also proposed and tested using the Real-World Modulation Dataset.

To validate deep learning algorithms in real-world settings, extensive testing is required on data from various hospitals and medical devices. For clinical applications like MS lesion segmentation, this necessitates vast datasets. A recent approach, the Learn Continually and Adapt (LCA) method, aims to learn from one dataset and enhance its knowledge with subsequent related datasets, thereby reducing the need for additional data. However, in clinical environments where labels are scarce, this strategy may not be practical. A comparison was made between LCA and an alternative method, the Learn Continually, Revert and Start Over (LCRvS) approach, using datasets from the MS-LES challenge. The LCRvS method was found to outperform LCA, suggesting that when labels are scarce, developing models on separate datasets might be a more effective solution.

We propose the contrastive manic learning framework, where a model generates diverse samples from its current distribution, evaluates them using a stable metric that doesn't change, and then adjusts the model only to maximize the metric's difference. By leveraging either Euclidean or KL-divergence, this approach prevents the model from overfitting and maintains a wide variety of outputs, making it effective in a wide range of tasks including image generation, inference, and evaluation.

The dynamics of complex systems are often analyzed using mathematical models, but model limitations can introduce unwanted biases in understanding these systems, particularly in predicting and analyzing their behavior. The effects of these limitations, combined with random noise, are inherent to any modeling process, yet there has been a lack of a structured approach to studying their impacts. In this study, a framework is developed to investigate the influence of model inaccuracies, incorporating the concept of a kernel function that represents random errors, irregularity, and structural limitations of a mathematical model, thereby simulating a unique type of noise that we term 'kernel noise'. The concept of kernel noise enables the examination of how model limitations and data precision affect our understanding of and predictions for the dynamics of growing systems, particularly in the context of modeling brain activity using spiking neural fields. Theoretical and numerical evidence is presented to demonstrate that increasing model limitations and noise levels can lead to the coexistence of identical outcomes with different origins, as well as the transformation of chaotic, aperiodic patterns into regular, periodic ones, and our analysis reveals a direct relationship between the type of errors, model limitations, and data precision, and the level of chaos exhibited by neural field models.

In the vicinity of the Sgr B2c molecular cloud, scientists have made a groundbreaking discovery of a previously unknown core, which they have dubbed Dragon. Located within the sphere of the Sgr B2c core, researchers have carried out a comprehensive study of Dragon using a range of observational techniques. By employing a combination of ALMA, IRAM, SOFIA, Spitzer, Herschel, Spitzer, Herschel, Gaia, and 2MASS data, they have gathered valuable insights into Dragon's physical properties. The data collected reveals that Dragon is a highly dense core with a peak density of 1.5e7 per cubic centimeter, as determined by CO emission. The evidence gathered also indicates that Dragon is undergoing significant expansion, with an expansion velocity of approximately 1.5 kilometers per second, as seen in multiple spectral line observations. The mass of Dragon has been estimated to be around 1.5e5 solar masses, as derived from 1.3 millimeter continuum data. The evidence also suggests the presence of a core expansion phenomenon, which is thought to be a result of the core's internal pressure. Recent studies suggest that dark matter might be composed of elusive particles that remain undetected despite extensive research. An alternative possibility is that dark matter consists of elusive microscopic objects, such as primordial black holes. If so, a significant portion of dark matter would reside within a significant radius of their core, where density is highest. In this region, we suggest that a new type of matter might emerge, which we refer to as shadow matter. This concept, which we believe could be a novel astrophysical phenomenon, involves the elastic scattering of dark matter within its own gravitational field. Here, we explore the concept of shadow matter by simulating the behavior of dark matter within a primordial black hole, taking into account its self-gravity. Our study utilizes the PopSyCLE code, which we have modified to include self-gravity, to model the elastic scattering of dark matter within its own gravitational field. Our preliminary simulations suggest that shadow matter could be a viable concept and potentially lead to the formation of stable, sub-planet-mass objects.

The concept of a fundamental building block for liquid crystals, a rigid wedge, has been further explored by a system of interlocking rigid wedges composed of spheres. Our research reveals that a unique state of disorder emerges, where the variations in spherical components lead to the out-of-plane distortion of the directional order. This unique state of matter bears resemblance to a fundamental characteristic of disclination structures found in traditional liquid crystals. Our findings suggest the potential for this system to exhibit distinct phases, including basic hexagonal and bicrystal configurations, as well as a disordered phase, where the out-of-plane distortion becomes pronounced. These novel states of matter possess potential applications in the development of advanced jammed granular materials and novel surface topologies.

Our goal is to fine-tune Large Language Models (LLMs) for specific tasks, like coding or generating math formulas, without overfitting and while keeping the number of adjusted parameters low. We've developed a new method called TASK TOKEN ADAPTATION (TASKAD), which uses a single, task-specific token to adapt LLMs. This method, when combined with a variant of Fine-Grained Few-Shot Prompting (FGFSP), achieves excellent results on multiple benchmarks, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques, especially under a very low parameter count.

Machine learning's success heavily relies on the continuous growth of datasets, 
which can be augmented by integrating relevant elements. Establishing a systematic 
prioritization for these components via preference ordering is crucial. In this 
research, a computational method for creating a non-contextual, binary preference 
order is explored. Next, the paper demonstrates how this ordering can be adapted 
to a contextual framework. Finally, comparative evaluations of contextual and 
non-contextual approaches using practical examples are provided through 
experiments.

The equilibrium thermodynamics of polymer liquids near the glass transition can be analyzed using a model based on a dynamic approach, specifically the equilibrium test-particle insertion method of Widom. We demonstrate in this analysis that a linear relationship exists between entropy, heat capacity, and test-particle free energy in the model. Moreover, our results indicate that an exponential relationship, as seen in entropic theory, exists between fragility and test-particle variance. The validity of the model is confirmed by comparing the predictions with existing experimental and simulation data.

This study showcases how a transformer-based language model can acquire rejection skills. By training the model to decline low-quality prompts, we found it can identify and refuse inappropriate inputs while maintaining high accuracy for suitable inputs. By integrating a pre-trained rejection module into the transformer model, we found rejection skills transfer effectively to previously unseen tasks. Evaluations on rejections of inappropriate inputs and inductive transfer to newly learned tasks demonstrate our findings. Our research contributes to a growing interest in exploring the capabilities of AI systems by focusing on developing general intelligence in artificial intelligence.

The emerging field of machine interpretation seeks to bridge the gap between black-box machine learning models and human understanding by generating readable and understandable English explanations. However, this task remains understudied and is complicated by issues such as the need to balance accuracy and interpretability, the importance of maintaining a natural language flow, and the challenge of crafting sentences that are both grammatically correct and semantically coherent. To address these complexities, this paper introduces a novel approach that capitalizes on look-ahead mechanisms to enhance the generation of explanatory sentences, using a pre-trained language model to guide sentence creation and prevent syntactic errors. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly improves the quality of the generated explanations and surpasses current state-of-the-art performance.

This study introduces an alternative calculation technique for the Kontsevich value of graph expressions, with a particular focus on graph representations of the symplectic泊松 bracket. Our calculation method yields the Kontsevich value of these graphs by employing the formal diffeomorphism theorem and properties of forests. Building on the new method, we establish the curvature graph identity of Kontsevich's theorem and subsequently calculate the Kontsevich value for the graph representations of the symplectic泊松 bracket identity. This value aligns with Li's formulae for Milnor algebras, as proven by Manin. Furthermore, we also examine the properties of multilinear graphs and their associated Kontsevich values.

We've developed a method to derive the thermal free energy for deformations of large-$N$ unitary conformal field theories in various dimensions. Our analysis reveals that deformations by operators with a slight suppression of large-$N$ cause the field theory to enter a deconfined phase, characterized by reduced symmetry, in contrast to the original fully symmetric field theory. Notably, this behavior stands in stark contrast to entanglement entropy in the same context. Our findings also indicate that, unlike entanglement entropy, thermal free energy doesn't necessarily decrease as large-$N$ reaches its limit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our deconfinement mechanism is not confined to large-$N$ but rather extends to classical theories.

Tan and Tan's 2007 paper introduced "a universal approach" for valuing Asian options in various financial markets. This note highlights the critical importance of the process X being a strong Markov process, and argues that the approach only functions effectively in specific, two-state scenarios. Additionally, the authors' claim of universality appears overly broad, as the approach solely applies to Asian options, not the broader category of path-dependent options.

The distribution of supermassive black holes in galaxies may be more significant to the universe than previously assumed. In a study, researchers used a unique model to simulate the universe's large-scale structure and the behavior of supermassive black holes in the most luminous galaxies in the universe. Their findings suggest that if the most luminous galaxies in the universe are primarily composed of supermassive black holes, the number of supermassive black holes in the most luminous galaxies in the universe is approximately one billion per cubic megaparsec. As a result, the most luminous galaxies in the universe would emit gamma-ray radiation that fills the entire universe and extends across vast distances over time. Simulations indicate that the supermassive black holes in the most luminous galaxies in the universe emit gamma-ray radiation that can be detected by future space-based observatories. In a specific scenario, the supermassive black holes in the most luminous galaxies in the universe emit gamma-ray radiation that can be detected in the energy range of 10 to 300 TeV. Their distribution follows a complex mathematical pattern and is influenced by the arrangement of galaxies in the universe.

In the early universe, non-linear interactions of primordial gravitational waves and their collisions with primordial curvature fluctuations can lead to unique patterns imprinted on primordial gravity, unobservable by traditional methods of cosmic inflation. A new research approach, the cosmological collider physics, has been developed to detect these patterns, which are believed to be present in primordial gravity but remain undetected. This study aims to introduce the concept of cosmic collider physics to a broader audience and create a conceptual tool for understanding non-traditional features of primordial gravity, which may emerge from non-linear processes in inflation.

This study aims to enhance the transparency and comprehension of how deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) function, specifically in the context of visual recognition tasks. Our approach centers on the observation that certain images contain distinct, discernible patterns or textures that are consistently identified by DCNNs, and that these patterns often correspond to specific, high-level concepts such as materials, structures, or types of features. By focusing on these underlying filters and their associated semantic meanings, we aim to shed light on the internal workings of these complex models.

The electronic behavior of one-dimensional cuprates is strongly influenced by interactions with phonons at both a local and broader scale. Within the one-dimensional Hubbard-phonon model proposed here, the electronic interactions are treated theoretically using a combination of bosonization techniques and numerical calculations based on Monte Carlo simulations. The electronic interactions are comprised of two distinct components: an attractive force extending over a long range facilitated by lattice vibrations and a repulsive interaction occurring close by. The competing forces result in the emergence of long-range ordered states, even within the constraint of one spatial dimension. The one-dimensional lattice structure tends to resist such ordering tendencies. The introduction of long-range phonon interaction greatly diminishes this resistance and enables the development of ordered states, even when short-range repulsion is strong.

The advancement of machine learning has been significantly influenced by the introduction of causal models, which offer more robust solutions by addressing confounding variables and reducing reliance on large datasets. Although numerous causal tools have been developed, the majority focus on extracting causal models from existing data. In this research, we explore the application of machine learning algorithms to automatically generate the structural components of a model's graph, specifically for the MPHIA dataset. We examine various scoring methods and Bayesian network learning algorithms to develop an accurate causal model. We also address the issue of handling variables with different data types in our research. We compare the effectiveness of our proposed methods with existing models in the literature and discuss the implications of our findings.

The phase diagram of the chemically disordered magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ was studied, which is unique for its coexistence of a metastable skyrmion phase and a conical ground state. Using a combination of numerical and analytical methods, the authors examined the effects of compression on the magnet's metastable topological structures. Their findings suggest that applying pressure can induce a phase transition from the metastable skyrmion grid to a cone-like ground state, which is in line with experimental results. Moreover, the researchers identified a potential mechanism for the disappearance of topological skyrmions, which involves their merging into larger cone-like metastable states. Furthermore, the authors proposed that further compression could stabilize these metastable cones temporarily, before they eventually become the ground state at high pressures.

In social network analysis, a widely used approach involves dynamic influence models. These models, however, become impractical when dealing with a large number of individuals, as they are computationally expensive and rely on simplistic assumptions. The introduction of a new class of models, which combines techniques from time-series analysis and network science, offers a promising solution. These models, however, are still in a research stage and require further development to address a range of methodological challenges. This article provides an overview of novel techniques aimed at influencing models in high-dimensional spaces.

The static point method, a simplified approach to partial differential equations, employs pre-determined values for function approximation without the use of specific basis functions. This paper examines the influence of static points on a linear first-order advection equation and demonstrates how their optimal positioning can minimize numerical diffusion. Our investigation reveals that, in order to mitigate diffusion errors, the static point method requires the selection of x-indices that correspond to the wave's spatial direction. This paper will lay the groundwork for a more comprehensive study of higher-order equations and a broader class of numerical methods.

A straightforward technique called $U$-reversible steganography allows for the hidden data to be transmitted without distortion after being retrieved from the transmitted message. The proposed approach utilizes a Bayesian neural network to create and decode a $U$-reversible code, where training only demands the sender's data. This method is efficient as it involves no additional parameters for decoding and incorporates a single global decoding parameter for the sender and receiver. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach using a variety of image and video formats, including JPEG, H.264 and MP4.

A mean-field approach to dynamo theory is widely used to study convective atmospheres, but its accuracy is compromised by the reliance on an oversimplified approach to separating large-scale and small-scale dynamos, which neglects a full range of turbulent effects. By applying direct numerical simulations to test mean-field convective models, it becomes apparent that the use of these models leads to significant discrepancies, with errors reaching up to two orders of magnitude, in their predictions of key dynamo characteristics. Consequently, the use of these models may result in misleading scientific conclusions. To counteract this issue, we suggest implementing a comprehensive set of constraints to ensure the reliability of mean-field convective dynamos.

A massive Galactic Center molecular cloud in the starburst galaxy NGC4945 has
ejected a smaller cloud approximately 100 astronomical units per year, possibly
due to an internal supernova explosion. This process has caused significant
changes in the cloud's morphology, driving a highly collimated outflow. A
distinct shock front, possibly due to a fast-moving shock front, separates the
ejected and remaining cloud. Analysis of CO and CS spectral lines reveals a high
velocity of the outflow and a shock front, with the latter indicating a high-
density gas. This process has been proposed as a mechanism for the formation of
dense gas in the galaxy, with the ejected cloud serving as a source of new
dense gas.

A novel time-dependent solver has been created for magnetized plasma models, which they apply to solve problems of nonlinear diffusion within complex magnetic field structures. Their approach is based on the finite element method and utilizes finite differences in time, with a specific emphasis on maintaining discrete energy conservation and positivity in magnetic fields through tailored numerical techniques. A specific application of this approach involves a modified version of the Galform model, with a step-by-step demonstration of its properties and validation via 2D test cases.

The SDIMSIM method employs a semi-discrete dynamical system to solve standard differential equations, incorporating an additional state variable that represents a continuous-time step. A previous version of SDIMSIMs had fixed step sizes, but in this study, we have developed a new variant with adjustable step sizes, maintaining fourth-order accuracy and stable behavior, even for problems with no explicit stiffness. The variable step sizes can be controlled through a simple criterion, independent of the problem's characteristics. The effectiveness of this improved method is demonstrated through comparisons with standard integration techniques and other variants of typical integration algorithms.

Inspired by a finding in H\"{o}nig and Staffans' work, we investigate the impact of perturbations on c0-semigroup generated solutions of Lyapunov differential equations within the framework of Banach spaces. We also explore the possibility of solving Lyapunov differential equations for positive, continuous, and compact operators in the context of Lp spaces with 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞.

The muon pair collider, a cutting-edge particle collider, is anticipated to significantly contribute to fundamental physics research, particularly in the investigation of the muon's magnetic moment, dimuonium-electromagnetic interactions, and the study of muon-based lepton flavor violations. To support dimuonium interactions with standard matter, we have developed MuMuPy, a comprehensive calculator capable of predicting the outcomes of muon-antimuon bound state interactions with various substances, including energy loss rates, and tracking the evolution of the muon pair's properties as it passes through different materials. This calculator, known as MuMuPy, provides precise estimates of energy loss rates and the progression of muon pair characteristics as they traverse different materials. To demonstrate MuMuPy's capabilities, we present example calculations of muon pair propagation through standard matter.

This paper explores investors' decisions on investing in a single risky asset, tracking two key metrics: the level of wealth relative to a minimum standard wealth and the period of time that wealth must remain above this standard. The focus is on the utility of the rich investor retaining their status, and we will eventually consider the equivalent of the rich investor's loss of wealth as the poorest wealth available. The utility function for this scenario will be modified and we will derive the best investment strategy under various conditions using advanced methods from calculus. Our results reveal that the rich investor should make bolder investment choices as their wealth increases, and more directly relate wealth to the minimum standard wealth, allowing for more aggressive investment when the minimum wealth is lower.

The formation of small galaxies is not yet fully understood, and current models suggest that the surrounding intergalactic medium plays a significant role in shaping these galaxies. However, the physical properties and chemical composition of this medium are largely unknown. Our research focuses on the cosmic cycles within the medium resulting from the formation of small galaxies in the first half of the universe's history, and we develop a model to predict its properties at the redshift of 0.5. The model reveals that the medium becomes increasingly metal-rich with higher redshift, containing about 0.15 times the solar metal abundance at the redshift of 0.5. The medium is composed of approximately 70% helium-4 and exhibits a ratio of total baryonic matter to stars formed of around 3.5. The results also indicate that the small-scale structure of the universe is largely composed of gas clouds with masses between 100,000 and 100 million solar masses. The temperature of these clouds is around 10 million Kelvin, and the pressure is approximately 10 million billion baryons per cubic centimeter. The predicted properties of the medium align with observations of the intergalactic medium in the vicinity of small galaxies.

A link operator can be used to connect local bosonic and fermionic systems, and it can be rephrased as a local constraint on the combined system's Hilbert space. This connection is similar to the fermionic constraint approach used in condensed matter physics. By applying two-dimensional weakly-interacting models with link operators, we can explore how the systems collapse under various conditions. Our calculations reveal two distinct collapse scenarios: the removal of bosonic degrees of freedom and a new type of collapse where fermionic degrees of freedom are removed instead, which occurs in one-dimensional systems and results in an effective interaction between the remaining particles.

This paper explores the properties of the central quotients of Thompson's groups F, T, and V in addition to their braided counterparts F_, T_, and V_ along with its subgroup V__ and the divergence behavior of these structures. Our investigation into the divergence of the centrally extended Thompson groups F, T, and V reveals that it is either a constant or varies at a logarithmic rate. This analysis also includes an examination of the divergence of the braided Thompson groups F_ and V_, which exhibit a similar pattern. In contrast, the divergence of the group T_ is equivalent to a polynomial function of degree one. Furthermore, the divergence of the subgroup V__ within V_ was found to be equivalent to the polynomial function x^1/3.

This paper provides a detailed explanation of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, incorporating the Deep Passage Search (DPR) component, to enhance the search capabilities of both search and retrieval models for in-depth queries. The framework, which combines external knowledge with language models, allows for improved model performance through targeted retrieval of relevant information based on external data and specific evaluation tasks. By training, evaluating, and fine-tuning the RAG framework, we achieve substantial gains over the DPR-only baseline on several search and reading comprehension benchmarks, demonstrating significant improvements in retrieval accuracy and model performance.

This study derives asymptotic expressions for the orthogonal polynomials and their reciprocals, considering a specific weight function defined as 1/(1 + x) over the interval [0, 1). We also identify the zero distribution and derive asymptotic expressions for Christoffel numbers and the Christoffel numbers of the first kind, in addition to constructing a strong asymptotic expansion for Christov functions. This asymptotic expression enables us to determine the location of the zeros and the convergence rate of the Christoffel numbers to their respective limits. Furthermore, by employing the Christoffel numbers, we develop a quadrature formula for integrals of the given weight function and derive the corresponding error estimates. Notably, the method used in this study is distinct from traditional approaches, primarily relying on the Stieltjes and Fourier transforms. This work serves as a special case for polynomials defined on the [−1, 1] interval with a similar weight function.

Human annotators play a crucial role in assessing the outputs of summarization models.
To identify the most qualified annotators, strict criteria are imposed on MTurk,
limiting the number of participants who can complete the task.
In an attempt to understand the process of finding such qualified annotators,
we investigated the recruitment process in detail.
Our research focused on the screening criteria used to narrow down the pool of candidates.
By analyzing a total of 1,000 MTurk participants,
we discovered that only about 10 individuals were eligible to take the summarization task,
and the remaining 990 were disqualified.
Notably, 80% of the participants were eliminated due to a specific question,
which effectively reduced the number of applicants by 80%.
Our study revealed that the screening process effectively reduces the pool of candidates,
but the effectiveness of the criteria used may not be optimal.
As a result, additional rounds of screening are required to identify qualified annotators,
consequently reducing the efficiency of the process.
Furthermore, we observed that the distribution of ages among the qualified and disqualified participants
is similar,
suggesting that the screening process is not effectively filtering out older participants.
Similarly, the success rates of participants across different demographics
are also comparable,
indicating that the screening criteria may not be the most effective in identifying qualified annotators.
